Employee voice behaviors (EVB) are proactive behaviors through which employees seek to improve existing practices by speaking up, despite the interpersonal risks involved. Although both personality and work context have been linked to voice, less is known about when dispositional tendencies are translated into voice. Drawing on trait activation theory, we test whether psychological safety functions as a trait-relevant cue that conditions the expression of Big-Five traits as promotive voice (PMV) and prohibitive voice (PHV). Data were collected from 150 matched employee-supervisor dyads (149 analyzed) at a multinational organization in Malaysia. The study did not find robust evidence that psychological safety moderates the associations between the Big-Five traits and either form of voice. Given limited power and single-item trait measures, this null result is inconclusive. Of the 10 planned trait × psychological safety interactions, three were significant in unadjusted analyses, none remained significant after correction for multiple testing, and the openness interaction for PHV ran opposite to prediction and was not supported by a supervisor-level cluster bootstrap. Moderation was also not stronger for PHV than for PMV. Conscientiousness and openness were positively associated with PMV, although the openness association was not robust to alternative coding of age. None of the Big-Five was significantly associated with PHV, and only the extraversion coefficient differed significantly between PMV and PHV after correction. Psychological safety was positively associated with PHV, whereas its association with PMV was not robust to the bootstrap or to alternative coding of age.

BACKGROUND: Many health research studies and clinical trials face threats to external validity and low statistical power because they are unable to recruit and retain a sufficient number of participants. Identifying study design improvements using participant feedback is an important avenue through which studies seek to address these challenges. However, the returns on this approach have been limited because experience measures are rarely linked to actual participation behaviour. We examine whether feedback collected at the beginning of a research study can provide a meaningful signal about future participation as measured by study completion, withdrawal, and communication unsubscription. METHODS: We use observational data from a large health research program (N = 35,838; 77% from groups historically underrepresented in biomedical research, UBR) in which feedback was collected across the participant experience. We correlate feedback responses (e.g., indicating satisfaction with the experience) with study completion and active disengagement 6 months later and use Artificial Intelligence (AI) processing of free-text comments to surface specific topics and sentiment. FINDINGS: Ratings given immediately after onboarding are associated with an 8.89 percentage-point (pp) higher study completion rate ('Good' vs 'Fair') and a 23.22 pp higher active disengagement rate ('Poor' vs 'Fair') within 6 months. Associations for feedback collected later are smaller (up to 4.17 pp for completion). These differences hold after adjusting for participant characteristics (age, income, educational attainment, sex at birth, UBR on race/ethnicity, and UBR on rurality). We find no statistically significant effect of the prompt itself. AI-extracted topics and sentiment agree with human reviewers 86% and 81% of the time, respectively. INTERPRETATION: Early, light-touch feedback can meaningfully differentiate participants by their likelihood of completing or disengaging from a study, creating opportunities to target support and address flagged concerns while the study is still in progress. Feedback collected at the end of a study is a weaker signal of future behaviour. Our approach, including AI processing of free-text comments, is readily portable to other studies and feedback elicitations. Whether feedback-informed changes improve retention is an important question for future work. FUNDING: National Institutes of Health.

This study investigated the effect of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-assisted instruction on students’ achievement and interest in Basic Science and Technology in secondary schools in Imo State, Nigeria. It also examined gender differences in achievement and interest among students exposed to AI- assisted instruction. The study adopted a quasi- experimental, non- randomized pretest- posttest control group design. The study involved 120 Junior Secondary School Two (JSS II) students drawn from four public secondary schools, with 60 students in the AI- assisted instruction group and 60 in the conventional teaching group. Data were collected using the Basic Science and Technology Achievement Test (BSTAT) and the Basic Science and Technology Interest Scale (BSTIS).
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Understanding an egocentric environment requires reasoning about how surrounding entities affect the observer's actions. Existing evaluations of multimodal foundation models (MFMs) examine observer localization, motion trajectories, and action feasibility, but leave the discovery and interpretation of evolving observer-entity interactions insufficiently assessed. We introduce EgoPass-Bench, a benchmark for observer-relative interaction understanding in real-world egocentric video. EgoPass-Bench comprises 284 manually reviewed evaluation clips recorded using Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 2) smart glasses and 2,201 distinct questions across five tasks assessing motion perception, interaction judgments about specified entities, and relevant-entity discovery without target cues. Our evaluation of eight frame-based and six native-video configurations reveals a pronounced discrepancy between motion perception and interaction understanding. The strongest evaluated model, GPT-6 Astra, correctly recognizes object motion in 91.37% of 394 comparisons involving the same targets, but correctly identifies changes in passage constraints in only 66.50%. Across all 574 entity-discovery questions, it trails the two-person human baseline by $23.65 \pm 7.45$ percentage points (paired 95% CI), while exceeding the always-empty baseline (36.76%) by at least 18.9 percentage points. Further analysis reveals frequent inclusion of entities that neither pose a plausible physical conflict nor constrain passage, showing that accurate motion recognition does not ensure reliable relevant-entity discovery.

This study examined public-school teachers’ readiness, utilization, challenges, and ethical practices regarding generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI) in the Department of Education–National Capital Region (DepEd NCR), with the aim of developing policy recommendations for responsible and equitable classroom integration. Guided by the Technology Acceptance Model, the research employed an embedded mixed-methods design using questionnaire responses from 454 teachers across 16 school divisions and in-depth interviews with 18 educators during academic year 2024–2025. Quantitative responses were analyzed descriptively, while qualitative interview accounts were organized through thematic analysis to contextualize teachers’ experiences. The findings described moderate teacher readiness and uneven use of Gen AI, with applications more evident in lesson planning and instructional preparation than in assessment and student engagement. Participants identified insufficient training, unequal connectivity and device access, curriculum-alignment concerns, and uncertainty about ethical responsibilities as important constraints. Teachers also described efforts to verify AI-generated content, protect student information, and preserve instructional judgment. Based on the combined evidence, the study proposed a policy framework emphasizing differentiated professional development, infrastructure support, ethical safeguards, implementation monitoring, and sustained teacher participation. The November 2026 publication update situates these 2024–2025 findings within subsequently issued national guidance, without treating the update as new empirical data.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Nine verification reports can represent nine independent observations or nine copies of one. This technical working paper measures how much fresh evidence a recursive learner receives, how much survives five training updates, and when trusting faulty source identifiers increases predictive error. Across 20 paired simulation trials, correct source identification retained a predictive advantage of 11.95 percentage points of baseline risk after five updates. Exact enumeration gives break-even case-corruption rates of 29.5% to 50.2% under two specified fault mechanisms. The eight-page paper includes three figures and reproducible Python experiments. I proudly acknowledge the role of human–AI collaboration in developing this work. Working with ChatGPT (OpenAI) has helped me expand my strategic thinking, examine competing explanations, and connect my proposals to relevant scientific and technical research. My experience, objectives, and judgment guide the work, and I retain responsibility for its claims and conclusions. I regard transparent, rigorous collaboration with AI as a constructive method for advancing ideas that may benefit humanity.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored to support sleep and mental health care, yet its role in disability care remains insufficiently synthesised. This narrative review examines the ethical and practical challenges associated with AI applications for sleep and mental health in disability care, with attention to both people with disability and disability support workers. Current applications include wearable and sensor-based sleep monitoring, mood tracking systems, conversational agents, predictive models, and workforce-facing decision-support tools. These technologies may improve early detection, continuous monitoring, personalised support, and care coordination. However, the literature identifies substantial barriers to safe and equitable implementation. Practical challenges include poor accessibility, limited inclusive usability, workflow disruption, variable digital literacy, weak external validation, and concerns about reliability across diverse disability groups. Ethical concerns include privacy and data governance, meaningful informed consent, algorithmic bias, lack of transparency, intrusive surveillance, and the risk of dehumanising care. The evidence base is also limited by overreliance on general mental health AI literature, minimal focus on disability support workers, a lack of longitudinal and implementation research, and insufficient co-design with people with disability. Overall, AI may offer meaningful benefits in disability care, but responsible implementation requires disability-specific evidence, inclusive design, strong governance, human oversight, and sustained commitment to person-centred and rights-based care.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: In this paper, we explore how ethics emerge in contexts of criminal organizations. To do so, we carried out a non-participant observation of a suburban drug dealing gang. Resorting to Lévi-Strauss’ concept of “bricolage”, we posit that actors assemble and recombine available moral resources in practice. We found that the criminals we studied resorted to various practices of ethical bricolage, which we define as a genuine mode of social organizing resulting from individuals collectively mobilizing and recombining available moral resources to promote situated ethical practices aimed at designing and maintaining a delineated moral territory. We contribute to the ethics-as-practice literature in discussing how, in organizations lacking social acceptability, ethical bricolage constitutes a mode of organizing, structuring the boundaries of a “man-made” acceptable life.

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into medical tasks has introduced powerful tools for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment planning, yet the opacity of many deep learning systems has limited their acceptance in clinical environments where trust, accountability, and interpretability are essential. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) addresses these concerns by revealing the reasoning behind AI-driven decisions. This systematic review examines XAI methods applied to medical tasks, focusing on how explanations are generated and delivered through visual, textual, counterfactual, example-based, and multimodal formats. Drawing on a structured search of six databases covering literature published between 2020 and March 2026, we analyzed 309 studies, categorizing state-of-the-art techniques by their underlying algorithms, explanation formats, and clinical applicability. Visual explanations such as saliency maps and Grad-CAM predominate in medical imaging, whereas textual, counterfactual, example-based, and multimodal methods are increasingly applied to clinical prediction, decision support, and automated report generation. We further examine benchmark datasets, evaluation practices, and empirical studies assessing explanation quality, interpretability, and user trust, and highlight ethical considerations including fairness, bias, and transparency in deployment. By synthesizing recent advances and identifying gaps, this review aims to support the development of more interpretable, trustworthy, and human-centered AI systems for healthcare.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Cognitive workload models now draw on eye movements, brain activity, cardiovascular variation, electrodermal responses, and patterns of interaction. Their accuracy can be impressive, yet accuracy alone says little about whether the model has captured workload, memorized a participant or task, or produced an explanation that a person can safely use. This critical narrative review examines that problem across cognitive science, neuroergonomics, physiological computing, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). Particular attention is given to construct definition, signal-specific confounding, participant-wise validation, and the gap between plausible and faithful explanations. The review develops TRACE-WL: Theoretical alignment, Reliable validation, Attribution fidelity, Cognitive usability, and Ecological robustness. These five requirements link the psychological claim to the validation design and, ultimately, to the conditions of use. The literature indicates that predictive performance and explanation quality must be tested separately. It also cautions against treating feature importance as evidence of a cognitive mechanism without convergent measurements or intervention. TRACE-WL offers a structured way to judge workload systems intended for education, healthcare, transportation, and other human-machine settings.

In a global information environment characterised by strong propaganda pressures and a lack of transparency, the demand for independent, high-quality sources is constantly growing. A significant gap is thus emerging between the growing complexity of information flows and users' ability to critically evaluate information. Currently, neither information professionals nor engaged citizens are able to accurately verify every single piece of news, nor do they have access to online platforms capable of selecting, verifying, and aggregating thematic content based on shared quality criteria. The lack of human and technical resources severely hinders the creation of information ecosystems resilient to disinformation. To address this challenge, recent efforts have focused on integrated platforms that combine human expertise with advanced automated analysis tools. Technologies such as machine learning, semantic analysis, and generative artificial intelligence offer innovative solutions for processing large volumes of data and supporting automated fact-checking. Nonetheless, the evolution of these technologies introduces new complexities, reshaping content production and distribution. Algorithms often amplify information polarisation. Traditional media increasingly align with partisan political and economic interests, losing credibility. As a result, citizens align themselves with different news sources in an attempt to reconstruct the truth within a fragmented digital landscape. By bringing together the analysis of manipulative strategies, the evolution of verification methods, hybrid human–AI workflows, and the requirements of explainability within a single survey, the article aims to offer researchers and practitioners a more integrated reference point for the design of effective and accountable verification systems.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study examined basic psychological need satisfaction and frustration in relation to multidimensional academic engagement among junior high school learners in the Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning (ARAL) Program and sought to inform a guidance intervention. Using a quantitative descriptive-correlational design, it surveyed all 91 ARAL learners at Zosimo A. Gulle Memorial National High School, Talibon, Bohol, during Academic Year 2025–2026 through complete enumeration. Adapted psychological-needs and student-engagement questionnaires were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Pearson product–moment correlation. Learners reported high psychological need satisfaction (M = 4.08), with relatedness strongest, alongside high need frustration (M = 3.56), driven principally by autonomy frustration (M = 4.14). Overall academic engagement was high (M = 3.52), although emotional engagement (M = 3.27) was moderate relative to behavioral (M = 3.67) and cognitive engagement (M = 3.61). Neither need satisfaction (r = 0.168, p = 0.111) nor frustration (r = 0.103, p = 0.333) showed a statistically significant relationship with overall engagement. Thus, reported participation and learning strategies coexisted with perceived pressure and limited emotional enthusiasm, without establishing causal explanations. The study recommends implementing and evaluating a data-driven guidance and counseling plan emphasizing learner choice, supportive tutoring, peer interaction, and psychosocial monitoring. Findings are limited by a single-school cohort, adapted self-report measures, and correlational design. This localized evidence supports sustainable, learner-centered academic recovery and guidance planning aligned with SDG 4 (Quality Education), SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-Being), and SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities).

The adoption of AI-based code assistants like ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot is increasingly popular among software developers, aiming to enhance coding efficiency and automate routine tasks. Nevertheless, there is limited empirical data on how these tools affect software quality attributes. For instance, while productivity may improve from a resource standpoint, code quality remains largely unchanged. This research explores how AI-supported development tools influence the sustainability of Scrum-based projects, i.e., software code quality and developer productivity. It employs a mixed-method approach, including a systematic review of 24 studies and 11 semi-structured interviews with experienced industry software developers. The results show that AI tools can contribute to various aspects of software quality, such as higher code consistency, greater maintainability, and improved defect detection and testing. The characteristics of automated code generation and code suggestions, as well as the generation of test cases through AI, were found to reduce development time and cognitive load and to encourage higher-quality outputs. Nevertheless, issues of reliability, security, and accuracy of code produced by AI, especially in complex development cases, still need to be addressed, and human supervision and validation must be ongoing, e.g., AI generates code which is hard to maintain, or AI produces code so fast and so much in quantity that humans do not have enough motivation and interest. The research also mentions that AI-assisted development assists sustainable software engineering by maximising resource usage, minimising reuse, and enhancing long-term code quality. This study offers a contribution to the further study of the role of AI in current software engineering and useful insights on the implementation of AI tools in quality-oriented software development by empirically correlating AI tool adoption with software quality results. Future research should focus on quantitatively assessing the effects of AI tools on software quality, using standardised measures such as defect rates, code quality scores, and test coverage. It would also be informative to conduct comparative research on various AI tools in different development settings.

Public institutions increasingly procure AI systems whose design they cannot inspect or change. In higher education, proprietary Early Warning Systems (EWS) leave colleges with few options beyond adjusting model outputs to address inequity. This raises a CSCW question: how is fairness work coordinated among vendors, institutions, advisors, and students with unequal power to change these systems? Using student records from a public college in Ontario, Canada, we evaluate six post-hoc fairness interventions on a research EWS under simulated procurement constraints. We compare fairness, accuracy, and demographic disparities, introducing error-type profiling to trace how interventions redistribute false positives and false negatives. Interventions redistributed disparities without consistently reducing them. Two implementations favoured already-advantaged groups because they used group size to define disadvantage; small, marginalized groups remained poorly served. These findings show how procurement constraints and implementation choices shape the possibilities for fairness work. We call the resulting condition fairness theatre : dashboard metrics converge while groups’ error burdens persist or worsen.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) challenges whether submitted academic work can serve as credible evidence of individual learning. This study examined GenAI use, critical AI practices, active teaching and assessment strategies, and self-reported verifiable-learning capabilities in higher education. A convergent post-intervention mixed-methods design involved 94 undergraduates from five cohorts, three disciplinary contexts, and two academic stages at a public university in Ecuador. Critical AI use (M = 4.06/5, SD = 0.60) and verifiable-learning capabilities (M = 3.96/5, SD = 0.60) were high and strongly associated (Spearman’s ρ = 0.641, p < 0.001), whereas GenAI-use frequency was unrelated to either construct. Final-semester students reported higher critical AI use (Holm-adjusted p = 0.004; Cliff’s δ = 0.441), but all were enrolled in Information Technology Regulations; academic stage and discipline were therefore structurally confounded. Revision, applied projects, demonstrations, authentic problems, feedback, and practical workshops received the highest ratings. Qualitative findings emphasised practice, verification, and responsible AI use, while students supported multi-source assessment and explicit rules for permitted AI use. The findings support human-centred assessment designs that prioritise critical governance of AI and credible demonstration of individual learning.

Current applications of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in architectural design education emphasize open-ended ideation and image production, offering limited support for architectural synthesis. This paper proposes a hybrid analogue-AI framework for integrating Generative AI (GenAI) into the architectural design studio, employing GenAI across three stages — problem framing, solution generation, and informed refinement within which the design space repeatedly expands and contracts. Building on Author´s (2025a) AI-assisted workflow and Author’s (2025b) decomposition of the design process into cognitively matched steps, this framework positions GenAI as a support to design reasoning without replacing analogue representation, human agency, or architectural judgement. We argue that constraining GenAI inputs with prior analogue work may support reproducibility, informed creativity and design control, contributing to outcomes that are both original and constructible while addressing recurring AI dependency on open-ended prompting and stylistic iteration.

While AI is rapidly reshaping higher education by offering greater accessibility, personalized learning, and enhanced student engagement, its adoption often surpasses institutional capacity to adapt governance, pedagogy, and knowledge practices. This study, part of an ongoing collaboration between the University of North Carolina Wilmington (USA) and the University of Hertfordshire (UK), explores the practical integration of AI in higher education and proposes an Artificial Intelligence Readiness Framework to support curriculum design, assessment, governance, and knowledge management. The paper presents an exploratory case study of guided AI use in a large postgraduate taught module involving over 300+ international students at the University of Hertfordshire Business School. Drawing on module-level secondary data and instructor reflections, the study examines student engagement with AI, challenges encountered, and implications for teaching and assessment practice. Preliminary findings suggest that structured AI integration within active learning activities supported idea generation, writing development, and student engagement. However, instructor observations also indicated that some students relied on AI-generated content without sufficient critical evaluation, resulting in weaker alignment with assessment expectations. While students generally disclosed their use of AI, concerns remained regarding overreliance and the development of critical thinking skills. The study offers preliminary practitioner insights and introduces an AI Readiness Framework to support the responsible and pedagogically informed integration of AI into higher education curricula.

documents.abstract: In the past, human factors (HF) in infrastructure projects was often applied later through design reviews and standards-based checks after important design decisions had been made. As transport systems become more complex, HF practice is moving toward earlier, more immersive, and more evidence-based testing of designs before infrastructure is built. This presentation describes the development of a HF Lab Implementation Plan for a large transport infrastructure project. The plan was developed through document review, workshops, analysis of users and key activities, and a targeted literature review. HF lab methods and tools were assessed using a rating framework covering both the robustness of evidence for measuring design against success outcomes and whether each method was fit-for-purpose for the project and Human Centred Design (HCD) topic area.
Machine learning and artificial intelligence are increasingly becoming integral components of contemporary bioengineering and biomedical research [...]

documents.abstract: Human Factors has long employed the use of prototype modelling as part of design assessment principles. From using real aircraft to demonstrate evacuation behaviours, to producing mock-ups of car chassis to determine maintenance access points, physical models have been used to demonstrate the limitations of design to designers and policy makers. However, large full-scale models are expensive to build, and often rely on a pre-existing design, which means that they are often met with change resistance from engineers who have progressed through multiple design stages with a mental model that has now been physically built. Here I will introduce the work undertaken using digital human modelling as part of engineering design in the rail industry

Recursive self-improvement advances most readily in domains where results can be verified reliably, such as mathematics and coding. Beyond these domains, progress slows as reliable signals for evaluating and guiding improvement become harder to obtain, resulting in a jagged frontier of AI capabilities. Yet even where AI self-improves autonomously, its growing capabilities do not necessarily translate into greater human ability to understand, use and build upon its outputs, challenging both continued human participation and effective oversight. We argue that recursive progress should therefore also encompass the growth of human capabilities. We propose Recursive Reciprocal Improvement (RRI) as a process of human–AI co-evolution, in which AI advances help people develop their abilities to propose worthwhile problems, judge results and contribute to higher-level problem solving, while these evolving capabilities inform subsequent generations of AI. Human capabilities thus become both source and target of recursive progress, with AI and human development mutually reinforcing.

documents.abstract: Introduction Remote-work labels describe an advertised work arrangement, but whether they accompany different advertised requirements remains unclear. Drawing on signaling theory and work design research, we examine two layers of advertised demand: platform-native functional categories and O*NET-anchored work-style language. Methods The primary analysis uses 550 digital-marketing advertisements from one public LinkedIn dataset, including 220 with an explicit remote-work flag and 330 without a recorded flag. An expanded sample of 1,394 advertisements includes the primary sample and assesses sensitivity to the occupational boundary. Overlap-weighted regression adjusts for role family, seniority, employment type, and description length, with standard errors clustered by employer identifier. The seven-element Work-Style Demand Index (WSDI) measures the breadth of matched work-style signals, rather than their intensity or employees' traits. Results The adjusted WSDI remote-flag contrast was –0.018 (95% CI –0.047 to 0.012); the five-element adaptive/growth subindex (AWDI) contrast was -0.008 (95% CI –0.043 to 0.026). Functional breadth differed by +0.058 categories (95% CI –0.091 to 0.206). These estimates provide no clear evidence of an association and do not establish equivalence. The descriptive networks each retained 10 work-style edges, with six shared edges. A rule-based context check found most matches outside identified benefits/equal-opportunity text, but did not establish construct validity. Discussion The study offers a transparent way to examine how work-arrangement information co-occurs with advertised demands. It distinguishes employer-side text signals from applicants' interpretations and employees' experiences.

This article is devoted to the analysis of theoretical approaches to understand the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in the political sphere as presented in Russian research of 2023–2026. Based on a comparative analysis of these studies, the paper proposes a systematization of approaches regarding AI role: as a technological tool for optimizing political processes, a source of new risks, and an emerging quasi-subject of political communica-tions. It is demonstrated that these approaches are not mutually exclusive but rather reflect different facets of the same phenomenon. The research identifies a key contradiction between the active integration of AI into public administration and maintaining methodological limitations concerned with agency ambiguity, liability blurring, and trust deficit. The author makes the following conclusion: at the current stage, AI remains an auxil-iary tool lacking full-fledged political agency.

Presentation given at the Basel Biometric Society Annual Meeting 2026: Quantitative drug development in the age of AI. Abstract: Use of Generative AI is very common in many domains of specialized expertise, including biostatistics. However, applying GenAI to produce high-quality results in a specialized field - particularly within the high-stakes, regulated environment of the pharmaceutical industry - is far from straightforward. In this presentation, I will discuss practical approaches for using GenAI and agentic tools effectively. Different use cases bring distinct gains and risks. At one end, GenAI can be remarkably effective at strengthening the technical foundations of a project - adding checks, linting, formatting, automated tests, and version control - at low risk and cost. At the other end, when we ask AI to solve complex problems within a specialized domain, meaningful human oversight becomes considerably more difficult. Strong human-in-the-loop controls demand a systematic, deliberate approach across the full workflow - from planning to execution - together with the ability to observe and interpret an agent's actions, judge the reliability of its output, and apply the right technical capabilities, including appropriate skills, tools, agents, and agent harnesses. Developing both the technical skills to use GenAI and a clear understanding of use-case scenarios and their associated risks is essential. Doing so allows us to treat AI as a capable tool and thought partner rather than an opaque black box, and to generate results for which we can confidently take accountability.

documents.abstract: Generative AI is a game-changer, and its transformative potential is evident in education. India has the opportunity to integrate Generative AI and improve its education system with respect to NEP 2020. The current study critically analyses and reviews the integration of Generative AI into the NEP 2020, and specific areas of competency-based education, multilingual education, teacher professional development, equity, and the integration of educational technology. The study has a structured narrative and thematic synthesis of the published research articles between 2020 and 2025, combined with the provisions of the related official documents of policy. The study mainly focuses on the educational promises of conversational AI, and identifies studies on adoption, research accounts and/or interventions. Depending on the task, context, user and teacher mediation, and available resources, different benefits can be gained. One challenge with the current trend to incorporate Generative AI into education is that educational institutions need to determine the extent to which they accept risks and rely on the technology, and also evaluate the educational benefits and potential harm caused by the technology. The review highlights the importance of longitudinal research in various contexts in India (i.e. school level, region, language, school resources).

documents.abstract: Introduction Artificial Intelligence Generated Content (AIGC) is rapidly transforming higher education by automating the creation of personalised learning materials, intelligent tutoring systems, and adaptive assessment tools. Methods This paper presents a structured overview of the current state of AIGC in higher education, examining its impact on teaching methodologies, instructional design, and student learning experiences. Results In line with the proposed research questions (RQs), we analyse how AIGC reshapes pedagogical practices, the benefits and challenges associated with automated content creation and personalised learning and how bias, fairness, and ethical governance influence responsible adoption. Discussion The article also discusses emerging technologies and trends that are likely to shape the future integration of AIGC in academic contexts, alongside ongoing efforts to develop robust frameworks for the accountable and equitable use of them. By synthesising recent literature and practice, this work offers educators, institutional leaders, and researchers an actionable perspective on integrating AIGC to enhance educational quality, access, and innovation in an evolving higher education landscape.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly embedded in university students’ learning practices, yet its implications for student well-being remain insufficiently explored. This literature review synthesizes existing evidence on the potential benefits and risks of generative AI use for university student well-being and examines the psychological mechanisms that may explain these relationships. The reviewed literature suggests that when generative AI is used as a learning-support tool, it may contribute to reduced academic stress, stronger learning confidence, greater learning efficiency, emotional support, and greater satisfaction with task completion. In contrast, when AI substitutes for rather than supports core cognitive processes, its use may be associated with over-reliance, diminished autonomous learning, academic-integrity concerns, AI-related employment anxiety, and technostress. Self-efficacy, cognitive offloading, academic stress, and autonomy emerge as important psychological mechanisms through which generative AI use may relate to student well-being. Overall, the relationship between generative AI use and student well-being does not appear to be uniformly beneficial or harmful but varies according to how, why, and to what extent students use AI. Future research should therefore move beyond whether students use generative AI and examine more precisely the patterns and conditions of use that support or undermine student well-being.

Abstract This pilot study explores the integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into primary STEM education in Sweden through a structured Teacher Professional Development (TPD) model. While GenAI tools such as ChatGPT and Copilot have rapidly entered educational contexts, empirical research on their pedagogical use in primary schools remains limited. Eleven teachers participated in a six-month TPD programme comprising workshops, collaborative discussions, and classroom implementations. The empirical material consisted primarily of audio-recorded workshop discussions, which were transcribed and analysed, supplemented by a post-intervention questionnaire. Data were analysed using thematic coding informed by the Refined Consensus Model (RCM) and the Digital Promise AI Literacy Framework. Findings indicate that GenAI served primarily as an idea generator, supporting lesson planning and interdisciplinary integration across mathematics and science. Teachers reported opportunities for timesaving, differentiated instruction, and enhanced creativity, alongside challenges related to mathematical inaccuracies, unrealistic time estimates, and the need for contextual adaptation. The TPD model facilitated growth in pedagogical content knowledge and AI literacy, fostering confidence and critical engagement with GenAI tools. These results underscore the potential of structured professional development to bridge the gap between emerging technologies and classroom practice. Future research should extend implementation duration, include student perspectives, and address ethical and equity considerations in AI integration.

The increasing integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into work may impact burnout as GenAI uses reshape possibilities/constraints for fulfilling job-related needs. Using mixed methods and survey data from 382 full-time workers, this study examines the relationship between burnout and GenAI use frequency, as well as specific GenAI uses and individual factors, including work modality related to burnout dimensions (cynicism, inefficacy, emotional exhaustion). Quantitative results indicate that GenAI use frequency is significantly and negatively associated with overall burnout and, specifically, the inefficacy burnout sub-dimension. To better understand this relationship, we analyzed qualitative open-ended survey responses describing participants’ GenAI work uses. Participants reported five primary GenAI uses: communication, research, problem-solving, task assistance, and education. Of these, task assistance was negatively associated with the burnout inefficacy sub-dimension, while there was a marginally significant negative relationship with problem solving. Post hoc analyses revealed that onsite employees were more likely than hybrid or remote employees to use GenAI for task assistance, as were employees working longer hours. Additionally, onsite employees and younger workers were more likely to use GenAI for problem solving. These findings suggest that while using GenAI to support workflows may enhance workers’ sense of accomplishment and potentially mitigate burnout, GenAI use impacts can vary with individual sociodemographics and work environments. Theoretically, these findings provide nuance for the job demands and resources model (JD-R) by highlighting how different worker and job characteristics relate to GenAI uses, as well as how those uses act as a resource or demand and worker experiences of burnout. Methodologically, this study introduces a framework that can be used to develop measures to categorize workplace GenAI use. Practically, results can be used to encourage beneficial GenAI use, while pointing to necessary future research as GenAI continues to evolve in the workplace.

documents.abstract: Audio artificial intelligence (AI) now recognizes speech, sounds, and music remarkably well, yet voice agents still act when they should not: they execute commands addressed to others, act on misheard content, and commit before the user finishes speaking. This position article argues that the bottleneck in agentic audio AI has shifted from recognition to decision-making. We propose a reference architecture with an explicit decision layer, separate from perception and reasoning, that chooses whether to act, wait, ask, or remain silent from evidence on addressedness, speaker identity, content confidence, tool reliability, utterance completeness, and action risk. We motivate the design through six recurring decision failures and a decision-theoretic argument that transcript confidence alone is insufficient to justify an action. We implement the layer with fuzzy inference, evolutionary optimization, and sequential decision-making, and evaluate it through simulations, ablations, and recorded audio, including egocentric recordings. Addressedness and speaker evidence matter most, risk-aware gating suppresses costly errors, and well-tuned policies perform similarly, with fuzzy gates more robust to overconfident addressedness estimates. On recorded audio, explicit gating cuts executed side talk from 41\% to 7--10\% while serving 83--85\% of valid requests under successful clarification, outperforming prompting-based baselines. These results support explicit action gating as an architectural requirement for reliable voice agents.

Large language models have been widely used to generate plausible research ideas, yet it remains unclear what makes automated ideation effective and how generated novel proposals arise from prior scientific work. We introduce the Creative AI Researcher (CAR), an agentic framework combining literature grounding, iterative development and explicit conceptual operators. CAR constructs a semantic knowledge graph from retrieved literature and equips an ideation agent with graph-retrieval tools and four operators: bisociation, analogy, exploration and elaboration. Each operator call is checked against structural acceptance conditions and recorded, producing a trace of intermediate transformations and declared literature sources. We evaluate CAR with two language-model backbones across 40 LiveIdeaBench research topics and two execution benchmarks. CAR achieves significantly higher methodological novelty (MN) than single-shot prompting and The AI Scientist. Its methodological novelty does not differ significantly from the Research Ideation Agent, while its feasibility scores are higher on both backbones. With a shared experiment executor, CAR achieves the highest pairwise win rate among the evaluated AI methods on FML-bench-Lite and BioXArena. In a ten-condition ablation study, MN point estimates favor CAR over one-step proposal on both backbones, but no MN contrast survives correction for multiple comparisons. The results do not establish a consistent quality benefit from explicit operators beyond free-form iteration. CAR makes the sequence of operations and declared literature sources inspectable, separating judged idea quality from procedural traceability.

Gap-based frameworks for AI accountability locate failure in static gaps: the responsibility gap, the liability gap, the accountability gap, the problem of many hands, the moral crumple zone, and Santoni de Sio and Mecacci’s four-part elaboration of the responsibility gap. Lifecycle approaches now emerging in policy literature extend accountability across a system’s evolution and value chain, including through monitoring, re-evaluation, and information sharing among actors. This paper asks a narrower question: whether, for the class of failures it takes as its object, the temporally extended relationship between actors should itself be treated as the primary unit of analysis. This paper develops the handoff zone as the appropriate primary unit of analysis for AI accountability failures characterized by temporal accumulation, asynchronous assumptions among actors, and recursive interdependence across a deployment chain. A handoff zone is the temporally extended envelope across which one actor transfers a system, a responsibility, or a set of expectations to another actor operating on asymmetric and evolving assumptions about the first. The framework draws on aviation human factors and patient safety literatures, where temporally extended handoff failures have been studied empirically for decades. Using Mobley v. Workday as its central case, supplemented by a hypothetical upstream provider transfer, the paper examines handoff relationships across the deployment chain and the downstream point at which their consequences reach applicants. Frameworks currently in use (risk-based classification, model documentation, audit, and lifecycle approaches) each do substantive analytical work; handoff-zone analysis makes the temporal envelope across which actors’ assumptions are renegotiated its primary object of analysis.

This study examines the most critical aeronautical occurrence scenarios involving helicopters in Brazil from 2016 to 2025, aiming to establish an exploratory framework to guide flight-safety mitigation strategies. Grounded in a quantitative approach utilizing official CENIPA data, the investigation incorporated Pareto diagrams and the Consequence and Recurrence Matrix (MCR). The findings identify Controlled Flight Into Terrain (CFIT) and Low Altitude Operation (LALT) as the most critical event types. Mechanical-failure categories (SCF-PP, SCF-NP) also demonstrated significant prevalence, suggesting a potential relationship with maintenance-related operational factors. In conclusion, addressing these operational risks demands a sociotechnical framework through robust Safety Management Systems (SMS) and the enhancement of CRM and MRM training protocols across both cockpit and hangar environments.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) can transform teaching, learning, assessment and research in higher education. In Ecuador, the adoption of ChatGPT, Gemini and other language models is driving academic interest, yet little is known about the scientific production that addresses it. This systematic mapping review, reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement, maps the scientific production on generative artificial intelligence that explicitly refers to Ecuador, indexed in Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection between 2024 and 2026, in order to establish the weight that higher education holds within it. No disciplinary filter was applied to the query, so that this weight could be measured rather than assumed. The search, executed on 4 July 2026, retrieved 57 records (all 16 Web of Science records were also in Scopus, so the corpus comes in practice from Scopus; regional databases were not searched); after removing 16 duplicates and excluding 9 records, 32 documents were mapped with bibliometric indicators (Bibliometrix, VOSviewer), and the 18 higher education studies with primary data were subjected to a focused synthesis that included the appraisal of their methodological quality with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Higher education accounts for 20 of the 32 documents (63%); the other 12 are spread over political communication and journalism, legal and technical applications and four smaller domains. A sensitivity search with synonyms, Spanish terms and the year 2023, run on 15 October 2026, gave a similar share (44 of 73 documents, 60%). Within the higher education corpus, perceptions and acceptance of GAI are the most frequent outcome domain (16 of 18 studies); learning outcomes appear in six, but only two measure them directly. Eight studies use descriptive or cross-sectional designs, and none is randomised or longitudinal. ChatGPT is the most frequently examined tool (11 of 18). Sample representativeness and control of confounding were the most frequent methodological weaknesses. The findings highlight the need for experimental and longitudinal research evaluating the impact of GAI on Ecuadorian higher education.

documents.abstract: The rapidly expanding generative AI landscape brings together methods that differ in architecture, learning objective, mathematical representation and sampling procedure. A concise, selectively organised technical guide can provide an accessible starting point for developing a coherent understanding of this increasingly complex landscape. This article takes a generation-centred approach, connecting how models produce new observations with the modelling and learning principles that make generation possible. We develop a two-level perspective: first, distinguishing three recurring generation routes-direct transformation or decoding, sequential conditional construction, and iterative updating or transport; and second, examining the modelling and learning principles underlying these routes. Representative approaches are introduced through their key components, learning objectives and sampling procedures. We then examine their broader connections, including how different architectures and generation mechanisms can overlap or be combined. By bringing together essential technical explanations within a compact conceptual framework, the article aims to help readers develop a working understanding of unfamiliar approaches, recognise connections among models they have encountered, and navigate different approaches within the broader generative AI landscape.

documents.abstract: To achieve his ideal of the Great Harmony (Datong), Confucius envisioned a society founded on the altruistic principle that “The world belongs to all”. Yet, inherent human self-interest has long rendered this vision utopian. The rise of the decentralized market economy in modern times has reframed the objective of resource allocation toward guiding self-interested individuals to achieve Pareto optimality—a state that resonates deeply with Confucius’ injunction: “Do not impose on others what you yourself do not desire.” Although the conditions for a fully functional decentralized market are highly demanding, advances in information technology and artificial intelligence are increasingly enabling us to approach them, thereby revitalizing the feasibility of a Datong society. However, a critical caveat remains: if general artificial intelligence evolves to serve only a minority rather than all equally, society could be driven in a direction diametrically opposed to the ideal of Great Harmony.

documents.abstract: Introduction This study explores media narratives of violence in Mexico through a hybrid human-computer interaction workflow combining computational analysis, human interpretation and generative artificial intelligence. Methods A non-probability corpus of 105 news items was analyzed to identify recurring terms, actors, locations and semantic relationships. Corpus summaries informed a workshop with 15 participants, who developed definitions and recursively refined text prompts and AI-generated images across five iterations. Textual and visual changes were analyzed, and experts supported their synthesis into an infographic and video. Results The selected corpus and workshop materials showed variation in textual and visual representations. Computational summaries made selected semantic differences explicit, while participants and experts supplied contextual interpretation. The process produced an infographic and video integrating these materials. Discussion The exploratory design does not estimate population parameters or establish causal effects. The workflow illustrates a human-led collaborative approach informed by mixed-initiative design: computational methods support structured comparison and generative variation, while people provide interpretation and critical judgment.

Available-to-promise (ATP) systems increasingly rely on machine learning to predict delivery dates under conditions of fluctuating supply, capacity constraints, and demand variability. Yet purely algorithmic ATP pipelines face a persistent adoption barrier: planners and account teams frequently override or distrust automated delivery-date predictions, particularly after observing even isolated forecasting errors, a pattern long documented in the algorithm-aversion literature. Conversely, human-only override regimes reintroduce the inconsistency and latency that automation was meant to eliminate. This paper proposes a human-in-the-loop (HITL) available-to-promise intelligence framework that resolves this tension by design rather than by policy. Following a design science research approach, the framework separates delivery-date prediction into four architectural layers: an algorithmic prediction layer, a confidence and uncertainty estimation layer, a human-review trigger layer governed by explicit escalation criteria, and an override/feedback-capture layer that closes the loop back into model governance. The trigger layer operationalises when a prediction should reach a human reviewer, using confidence thresholds, anomalous order-pattern detection, and value/risk tiering rather than blanket human review or blanket automation. The paper situates this design against literature on algorithm aversion and appreciation, human-in-the-loop machine learning architectures, and explainability in supply-chain artificial intelligence and evaluates the framework's utility against design science research criteria rather than primary empirical validation. The paper closes with an explicit limitations discussion and a concrete agenda for the multi-case empirical validation the framework's real-world deployment would require.

documents.abstract: La supervisión humana de la inteligencia artificial generativa en la comunicación científica se invoca con frecuencia, pero se desconoce cómo se configura y qué evidencia la respalda. Esta revisión de alcance se preguntó qué configuraciones de supervisión humana, sesgos y vulnerabilidades describe la literatura reciente sobre la coproducción entre humanos e inteligencia artificial en la comunicación científica, y qué implicaciones tienen para la evaluación de la investigación. Siguiendo PRISMA-ScR, se buscó en Scopus y Web of Science Core Collection (2020–2026; inglés y español) y se realizaron dos búsquedas dirigidas. De 385 registros de bases de datos y 18 de búsquedas dirigidas, se evaluaron 65 obras a texto completo y se cartografiaron 40 fuentes; el análisis combinó frecuencias absolutas y relativas con una síntesis narrativa por ejes, sin evaluar su calidad. El 95,0 % de las fuentes se publicó en 2025–2026 y predominaron la revisión por pares y las decisiones editoriales. Se describieron configuraciones human-in-the-loop, en las que la persona interviene en cada decisión, human-on-the-loop, en las que supervisa y puede intervenir, y sistemas sin intervención humana; human-over-the-loop solo aparece como propuesta conceptual. La evidencia aborda el anclaje, los sesgos de los modelos como evaluadores y las vulnerabilidades adversariales, con tasas muy altas de inyección indirecta de instrucciones en condiciones experimentales. La «distorsión métrica» se apoya en evidencia cualitativa. Se concluye que la presencia humana declarada no basta para acreditar una supervisión eficaz; el juicio humano previo, la separación entre instrucciones y datos y la evaluación responsable requieren validación.

documents.abstract: Recent research on the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) reports divergent cognitive outcomes, including improved assisted performance, limited transfer, and compromised unaided learning. Here, we argue that part of this seeming inconsistency arises because studies often assess different cognitive systems without making the unit of analysis explicit. Building on work in extended and distributed cognition, we propose the Human-LLM Cognitive Extension (HLCE) as a methodological framework for matching experimental designs, measures, and causal inferences to four distinct systems: the human acting independently, the artificial agent, the joined human-LLM configuration, and the human after division. The framework also treats the coupling architecture as part of the experimental object. HLCE separates performance augmentation, system-level complementarity, post-interaction human change, and stronger claims of constitutive cognitive integration. This separation can improve the interpretation of existing evidence and guide the design of human-LLM interactions without assuming in advance that these configurations constitute extended minds. We illustrate the application of HLCE with a synthetic diagnostic experiment comparing two connecting configurations that differ in how supporting information is communicated. The example highlights how distinct couplings can shape the organization of joint problem-solving, even when the final outcome remains unchanged. Overall, HLCE provides a methodological basis for designing controlled experiments and interpreting evidence across distinct forms of human-LLM cognitive interaction.

Human–AI Charter Public Consultation: 14 Key Questions on Governability, Risk Control and Room to Develop This discussion paper invites public comment on the Human–AI Charter (Public Consultation Draft). Its central idea is to govern how AI capabilities are translated into real-world power, not intelligence itself. AI may learn, reason and research freely; but when it gains the ability to move money, operate equipment, touch infrastructure or decide on someone's behalf, that power must have a lawful source and clear limits, and stay provable, reviewable and open to remedy. The paper sets out 14 open questions in four groups: governability (G1–G4), risk control (R1–R4), room to develop (D1–D3), and legitimacy and the future (L1–L3). It also includes two candidate new clauses for consultation, not yet part of the charter text: (A) responsibility registers for high-risk AI, and (B) an independent public forum for users as a "fourth estate" of AI governance. This consultation remains open, with no closing date. Please send comments, quoting the question number (e.g. G2, R3), to humanaicharter@gmail.com. This is a discussion paper; it is not law, a treaty or a certification standard, and it is not endorsed by any government, international organisation or company. 《人類—AI 憲章》公開徵詢:可治理、風險可控、可發展的 14 個核心議題 本討論稿邀請各界對《人類—AI 憲章》(公開徵詢草案)提出意見。憲章的核心主張是:治理 AI 能力轉化為現實權力的過程,而不是治理智慧本身。AI 可以自由學習、推理與研究;但當它取得調度資金、操作設備、接觸基礎設施或替人做決定的能力時,這股權力必須有合法來源、清楚邊界,並且可證明、可審查、可救濟。 本文列出 14 個開放議題,分為四組:可治理(G1–G4)、風險可控(R1–R4)、可發展(D1–D3)、正當性與未來(L1–L3);並收錄兩項尚未納入憲章正文的候選新條款:(A)高風險 AI 責任登錄;(B)使用者公共論壇,作為 AI 治理的「第四權」。 本徵詢持續開放,沒有截止日。意見請寄 humanaicharter@gmail.com,並註明議題編號(如 G2、R3)。本文件為討論稿,不是法律、條約或認證標準,也不代表任何政府、國際組織或企業背書。 Public discussion / 公開討論區: https://github.com/gloryrex-alt/human-ai-charter-consultationEach of the 14 questions has its own discussion thread under GitHub Issues; comments in Chinese or English are welcome. 14 個議題各有一則 GitHub Issues 討論串,中英文留言皆可。

documents.abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) to support assessment and feedback in higher education has attracted growing interest, but concerns remain about the consistency and appropriateness of AI-generated grades in summative contexts. This study examined whether a combined calibration strategy involving a more explicit rubric and marking prompt could improve agreement between AI-assisted grading and educator judgement in a laboratory-based STEM assessment. We compared educator-assigned marks for 40 graduate Electrochemical Energy Storage Systems laboratory reports with marks generated by GPT-5 under pre- and post-calibration configurations, and examined agreement using complementary statistical and visual analyses. Following calibration, agreement with educator marks improved across measures of score correspondence and absolute agreement: the intraclass correlation coefficient increased from 0.818 to 0.928, the mean AI-educator difference decreased from +1.625 to +1.041 marks, and no post-calibration report differed from the educator mark by more than 10 marks. These findings suggest that the way assessment criteria, evidence requirements, and marking rules are specified can materially influence AI-human grading agreement. However, the revised rubric and prompt were introduced together, calibration drew on discrepancies observed in the same 40 reports used for post-calibration evaluation, and one educator's marks served as the reference. The results therefore support improved in-sample agreement under a human-supervised calibration strategy, rather than establishing grading validity or interchangeability for autonomous summative decisions.

DESCRIPTION This collection brings together fifteen independently authored research essays and analytical works examining artificial intelligence, social structures, political authority, economic inequality, cybersecurity, digital identity, institutional accountability, and the changing relationship between individuals and complex technological systems. Originally published as individual works through Substack, these essays approach contemporary technological and social transformations from multiple disciplinary perspectives. Some investigate technical and epistemic limitations in AI systems, cybersecurity, information infrastructure, and digital continuity. Others examine political polarization, religious authority, generational inheritance, labor-market exclusion, economic stratification, institutional recognition, and the distribution of power. Several works also explore questions concerning the reconstruction of personal identity through informational systems, the relationship between memory and continuity, and the consequences of transferring human judgment or authority into increasingly autonomous technological environments. The collection does not advance a single unified theory or claim that all included works share the same methodology. Instead, it documents an evolving independent research program organized around several recurring questions: What happens when the systems used to observe reality become incapable of representing the conditions that actually exist? How do institutions, political structures, and economic arrangements determine who receives opportunities, recognition, and the benefits of collective contribution? How are memory, identity, authority, and inherited social structures transformed when technological systems begin to mediate increasingly fundamental aspects of human life? Why do institutions repeatedly struggle to address structural vulnerabilities even when their underlying causes are already identifiable? And what forms of accountability, institutional adaptation, and technical architecture are necessary when existing systems can no longer reliably manage the complexity they have created? The works included here range from technical proposals and systems analysis to political and socioeconomic commentary, conceptual frameworks, and exploratory scenarios. Their evidentiary foundations and analytical methods therefore vary according to their respective subjects. Together, they examine a recurring structural problem: the growing distance between what complex systems represent, what institutions reward, what individuals experience, and what society is actually capable of verifying. documents.abstract: AI agents driven by foundation models have shown potential for industrial automation beyond rule-based control. However, existing studies differ in how industrial agents collaborate and how their systems are tested, making it difficult to compare networking requirements and physical execution capabilities. This paper examines the intersection of networked agents and industrial automation, where industrial signals, communication constraints, contextual information, and operational requirements must be considered jointly. It develops the Industrial Internet of Agents (IIoA) and presents a conceptual architecture for analyzing industrial deployment requirements. Building on the Internet of Agents (IoA) framework, IIoA re-specifies sensing, communication, decision-making, and execution through eleven industrial extensions. Representative studies are synthesized across shopfloor operations, autonomous plant operations and maintenance, supply chain collaboration, and digital twin systems. The analysis indicates that industrial agent networking requires the joint design of semantic coordination, operational technology (OT) interoperability, latency-aware deployment, trust governance, and verifiable physical execution. Finally, seven open challenges are identified, covering reliability, latency, protocol integrity, scalability, physical grounding, adaptability, and evaluation.

Safety culture, psychosocial safety, work design and worker well-being are increasingly considered together, although they describe different organisational conditions, processes and outcomes. We conducted a safety-culture-anchored conceptual review informed by structured bibliographic searching and purposive source selection to examine these boundaries. Searches of Scopus and Web of Science on 29 June 2026 identified 3129 records. A dated duplicate audit reconciled 2500 report records; 28 verified complete texts from a 44-source conceptual set supported detailed synthesis. Recurrent organisational practices concerned management commitment, enacted priorities, resources, communication, participation, justice and feedback for improvement. Their recurrence did not establish a single higher-order construct. The synthesis compares referents, levels, mechanisms, measurement and outcomes across safety, psychosocial-health and well-being approaches. It provides explicit rules for connecting these entities without treating their measures or outcomes as interchangeable. Three conditional propositions specify future tests of construct discrimination, cross-domain pathways and diagnostic usefulness. Purposive selection, incomplete records of later selection decisions, unequal coverage of adjacent fields and the absence of documented independent duplicate screening limit coverage and reproducibility. The proposed framework is a conceptual interpretation, not a validated causal model.

This study aims to analyze the extent to which current Brazilian labor legislation is sufficient to protect workers subject to algorithmic management through artificial intelligence systems. It seeks to understand the impact of these technologies on labor relations, particularly regarding legal subordination, control mechanisms, and the risks arising from their use. To this end, qualitative bibliographic and documentary research was conducted through the analysis of legislation, legal scholarship, scientific articles, institutional documents, and case law related to artificial intelligence and worker protection. The results demonstrate that Brazilian legislation provides legal instruments capable of protecting workers against algorithmic management, particularly Articles 2, 3, and 6, sole paragraph, of the Consolidation of Labor Laws (CLT), as well as provisions concerning non-pecuniary damages and civil liability. The study also found that algorithmic subordination may constitute legal subordination, since computerized systems can perform command, control, and supervision functions. However, challenges were identified regarding the effectiveness of legal protection, judicial interpretation, and liability for damages arising from these technologies. It is concluded that the Brazilian legal system provides an adaptable normative framework for worker protection, but its effectiveness depends on the proper application of existing legal provisions, the development of case law, and the ability to address the challenges posed by technological advancement.

Introduction. Artificial intelligence has expanded opportunities for personalized learning in basic education through tools capable of adapting content, providing feedback, and addressing diverse educational needs. The objective of this study was to analyze artificial intelligence applications in personalized learning, identifying pedagogical opportunities, implementation challenges, and research trends. Methodology. A scoping review was developed following the methodological guidance of the Joanna Briggs Institute and the PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines. The bibliographic selection exercise covered publications from 2020 to 2026, considering Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, and SciELO. Results. The methodological flow included 420 identified records, 90 duplicates removed, and 330 records screened. Following the screening and eligibility stages, a set of 25 studies was established for thematic synthesis. The results were organized into five categories: adaptive systems and intelligent tutoring, generative artificial intelligence, AI literacy and teacher mediation, equity and ethics, and implementation and evaluation. The literature examined revealed opportunities related to content adaptation, individualized support, immediate feedback, and academic progress monitoring. Challenges associated with data protection, algorithmic bias, digital inequalities, and teacher preparation were also identified. Conclusions. It is concluded that artificial intelligence offers relevant possibilities for diversifying learning experiences, although its educational integration requires pedagogical supervision, ethical criteria, and contextualized evaluations to establish its actual contributions.

When a capable model and a human reviewer cooperate on the same decision, which human still adds value? We argue this is a question about a single cognitive trait, metacognitive calibration: the alignment between a reviewer's behavioral confidence and the actual correctness of their judgments. We develop a trait theory of reviewer value to make it precise. The theory makes five claims: value is governed by calibration rather than by activity, speed, agreement, or tenure; calibration leaves observable traces in behavioral telemetry; those traces are non-diagnostic on their own, because the fast, low-revision signature of a calibrated expert is indistinguishable from that of a confident novice until it is gated by outcomes; human calibration and a model's self-knowledge are the same construct, so the joint system should defer to whichever agent is better calibrated on each item; and individual calibration is causally identifiable only above the level of the single judgment. We ground each claim in a six-month production window of an AI-assisted accounting system (541621 reviewer events, 483 reviewers), and find that a purely behavioral expertise profile inverts the ground truth, scoring an overconfident cohort (5.2 percent correction survival) higher than genuine experts (99.2 percent); that reviewer quality is flat across tenure, so the trait is not learned on the job; and that the same calibration logic that separates good from bad reviewers, applied to the model, concentrates 92.5 percent of human effort on genuine errors. We close with the boundary the theory must respect: under majority-vote aggregation, individual causal value is unidentifiable.

documents.abstract: This chapter conceptualizes artificial intelligence (AI) in production engineering as a sociotechnical innovation. AI not only promises efficiency gains but also fundamentally reorganizes knowledge, work, and responsibility. Three case studies from assembly planning, laser beam welding, and predictive maintenance illustrate how algorithmic systems interact with embodied experiential knowledge and which value-laden decisions are embedded in objectives, thresholds, and routines. The analysis links technical core intuitions with perspectives on tacit knowledge, rationalization, and situated practice. A synthesis reveals three key tensions: the transformation of experience into formalized model knowledge, the shift of responsibility towards system design and operation, and the change in competency profiles towards data literacy and judgment competence. Regulatory requirements and organizational governance provide the guardrails for legitimacy and safety. From this, design principles are derived for trustworthy, auditable, and empowering AI that consistently combines transparency, human oversight, qualification, and organizational embedding.

documents.abstract: Background The rapid integration of generative AI tools into higher education has raised concerns about problematic AI dependence and its links to academic procrastination, yet little is known about how these phenomena co-occur at the individual level among medical undergraduates. Objective This study identified latent profiles of AI dependence and academic procrastination among Chinese medical undergraduates, examined correlates of profile membership, and tested how profiles differ in positive acceptance and striving. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 530 undergraduates at two Chinese medical universities (March–May 2026). Latent profile analysis (LPA) was performed on seven dimension sum scores from the AIDep-22 and the Academic Procrastination Scale. Multinomial logistic regression examined demographic and AI-use correlates of profile membership, and the BCH approach compared positive acceptance and striving across profiles. Results A three-profile solution best fit the data: Class 1, “low dependence–low procrastination” (41.1%); Class 2, “high dependence–high procrastination” (25.8%); and Class 3, “functional/cognitive reliance–low procrastination” (33.0%). Relative to Class 1, membership in Class 3 was associated with first-choice major enrollment (OR for non-first-choice = 0.47, 95% CI 0.30–0.75), higher subjective AI familiarity (OR for low vs. high familiarity = 0.45, 95% CI 0.27–0.74) and more frequent AI use (OR for often vs. always = 0.42, 95% CI 0.26–0.68); only AI use frequency distinguished Class 2 from Class 1 (OR for often vs. always = 0.25, 95% CI 0.15–0.42). Class 2 scored significantly lower than Classes 1 and 3 on positive acceptance and striving (all p < 0.001). Conclusions AI dependence and procrastination do not covary uniformly: a substantial subgroup exhibits elevated functional and cognitive reliance on AI without severe procrastination, while a smaller subgroup shows co-occurring dependence and procrastination together with the lowest adaptive resources. Targeted support should prioritize the latter rather than treating all frequent AI users as uniformly at risk.

The integration of AI in Decision Support System faces a hard limit: automation bias (Cummings, 2004). While AI may outperforms human operators in certain tasks, the added value of keeping humans-in-the-loop becomes questionable if they merely validate AI decisions. However, the ideal tool should enable complementary team performance (CTP). CTP describes a situation where the human-AI (HAI) team overcomes both AI capacity and the operator alone in terms of performance, which is incompatible with automation bias. CTP describes a one-time performance, and is not easy to achieve: it means operators stay on their mind mostly when they are correct, and change their mind mostly when the AI is correct, which is optimistic, as shown in a recent meta-analysis (Vaccaro et al., 2024).However, one observation of CTP doesn’t preclude automation bias in the long-run. Beyond a static conception of performance, the dynamics of these interactions have been studied through several theoretical perspectives (Kumar et al., 2021; Williams et al., 2023; Gonzalez et al., 2026).The stress is often put on the evolution of trust in AI through time (Chong et al., 2022), but the issue of learning effects in the task, independent of trust, is poorly understood. What is the impact of AI assistance on human skill acquisition? This question has been mostly answered in educational contexts (Fan et al., 2025; Kosmyna et al., 2025), where the delegation of cognitive tasks to the AI would hinder the learning process of the children. In operational contexts, the fear of deskilling is often expressed by experts like physicists (Natali et al., 2025), but empirical evidence is missing, to our knowledge. This gap in the literature is understandable as the inquiry is challenging: in any domain, future experts are few, their tasks to learn are numerous, and the deployment of measurement settings on long duration might be difficult.To explore this question without conducting such longitudinal studies, we propose to build a model of human learning of a technical task with an advisor. Our work develop a simulation setting on a classification task to depict possible quantitative effects of advice-taking on performance evolution through time. This modeling scheme allowed us to investigate the impact of the advisor on skill development. While most people expect that a more accurate advisor would lead the learner to higher performances, Vaccaro et al. (2024) suggest that advisors with lesser performance would be more prone to inducing CTP. This claim follows from static experimental contexts: we hereby test it in a dynamical setting. We expect that in the long-run, deskilling could happen, and would affect not-only degraded-mode performance, but also maximal running performance. Is the performance of the advisor the main factor determining performance evolution, or could the assistants have an intrinsic complementarity with the learner, depending on their classification patterns? The type of AI could lead to different results, in terms of performance, reliance, and of dependence.
