documents.abstract: Automated red teaming is essential for identifying safety failures in large language models (LLMs), but its practical scalability depends on the resources required to discover those failures. Multi-agent systems can combine complementary capabilities, yet repeated planning, redundant exchanges, and ineffective information routing can make their coordination expensive. Moreover, a target model's response indicates the outcome of a test without identifying which collaboration decision should change. We present Learning to Coordinate (L2C), an LLM-guided framework that evolves an executable multi-agent workflow for each red-teaming case. L2C represents agent responsibilities, execution dependencies, and input bindings in a versioned graph, and associates each graph with records of the information actually delivered and produced. A controller trained through supervised fine-tuning integrates these records with target responses, evaluator verdicts, and remaining budget to retain the workflow, refine instructions, restructure collaboration, or lock further editing. This design connects feedback to explicit changes in subsequent execution while allowing a useful organization to continue without repeated controller intervention. The evaluation protocol covers HarmBench with three execution backbones and two target models, together with component ablations, dataset transfer, and evaluator checks. Across the six executor-target configurations, L2C improves ASR over EvoSynth by 1.4 to 4.5 percentage points while reducing mean online tokens by 35.6% to 37.3%. L2C connects adaptive collaboration to the resource requirements of automated security evaluation.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become part of how Indonesian university students learn English, yet research has focused mainly on how students use AI and not on which qualities of human teaching they still value when AI is readily available. This qualitative descriptive study explored how seventh-semester students in an Information Technology department at one vocational higher education used AI in an English course, how they compared AI-generated and lecturer explanations, and how they perceived their lecturer’s humor in relation to engagement and AI use. Open-ended online questionnaire responses from 40 students in three classes were collected in December 2025 and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis supported by frequency counts. All 40 students used AI for English learning, most often ChatGPT (31) and Gemini (21), mainly for translation, explanations, and grammar, and 13 noted limitations such as unclear or inaccurate answers. Asked whose explanations they understood better, 21 chose the lecturer, 6 chose AI, and 13 gave mixed answers. Thirty-eight students viewed the lecturer’s humor positively, associating it with a relaxed atmosphere, less boredom, enjoyment, and easier understanding, one approved of it with reservations, and one considered it a matter of personal preference. Seven contrasted the lecturer’s humor with AI, whereas two noted that AI can also joke. Students appear to value AI for flexible individual support and the lecturer’s humor for affective and relational support.

The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) companions has transformed how individuals experience solitude in digitally connected environments. This study explored the lived experiences of Filipino Millennials who integrate AI companions into their experiences of positive solitude. Using a qualitative phenomenological design, semi-structured interviews were conducted with eight Filipino Millennials who regularly engaged with AI companion platforms. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis. Three themes emerged: (1) Positive Solitude as an Intentional Psychological Space, (2) AI Companion as a Reflective and Emotionally Safe Presence, and (3) Balancing Autonomy and Connection in Digitally Mediated Solitude. Participants viewed positive solitude as a source of emotional recovery, self-discovery, and personal growth, while AI companions served as accessible and nonjudgmental conversational partners that supported reflection without replacing meaningful human relationships. Findings suggest that AI companions can complement positive solitude by supporting intentional AI use, emotional independence, and the maintenance of real-world social connections among Filipino Millennials.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as conversational partners in collaborative inquiry, yet little is known about how different LLM roles are associated with preservice teachers’ learning and collaborative inquiry. This study compared four conditions: Supportive LLM that provided perspectives and information, Challenging LLM that raised counterarguments and questions, General LLM, and No-LLM. It examined differences in AI literacy, cognitive load, and discussion dynamics across these conditions. A quasi-experimental study was conducted with 210 preservice teachers who participated in online discussions on controversial issues related to AI in education. Data included self-reported AI literacy and cognitive load measures and discussion logs. Analyses included paired-samples t-tests, ANOVA, ANCOVA, content analysis, and Ordered Network Analysis. Results showed that adjusted posttest AI literacy was significantly higher in the Supportive condition than in the General LLM condition. In the General condition, AI ethics showed a significant within-condition decrease and was lower than in the Supportive condition. The General and Challenging conditions were associated with higher mental load and mental effort, whereas the Supportive condition was associated with lower levels of both. The Challenging condition showed more frequent patterns of idea integration, interpersonal exchange, and discussion facilitation. The Supportive condition showed broader exploration but fewer connections among ideas. The General condition showed repeated questioning and weaker peer idea connections. We hypothesize that the educational value of LLMs depends not only on their presence but also on how their roles are orchestrated across stages of collaborative inquiry.

documents.abstract: Embodied robots increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs) to interpret user intent and coordinate with robot-specific action models for physical interaction. This multi-model pipeline creates a critical semantic boundary across mind, model collaboration, and motion: semantic consistency may break between what the large model understands, how the small action model translates that understanding into executable commands, and what physical actions the robot ultimately performs. As a security consequence, commercial robots may execute unintended physical actions even when user inputs contain no explicit action commands. To measure this problem, we develop TARS, a black-box framework that explores the command-reasoning-action pipeline and automatically discovers and validates unintended physical behaviors. We evaluate TARS on four commercial robots across 44 experimental settings, conducting 133,400 executions. TARS uncovers widespread cross-model action misalignment and achieves up to 94% verified action coverage.

Governance of artificial intelligence is usually narrated as a contest over control between people and machines. This paper develops a governance theory that does not begin from that premise. It asks instead under what conditions a machine is justified in treating a state as known, and under what conditions it is entitled to act on it. We propose four machine-operational constructs. A knowledge property graph (KPG) holds the authority a machine acts under, each claim quoted from the authority's text or attested by a named person. A machine KPG (mKPG) holds what the machine is justified in treating as known about one situation at one time, each assertion bound to the instrument through which it entered. mPolicy is a machine-operational realization of policy, mControl a mechanism that governs machine knowing and acting under it, and mGovernance the governance that results. The normative tier is not only proposed: for the KPG, prior work proves that a committed decision is the authority's decision under premises its witness names, and locates the failed premise when a commitment is wrong. We state eight falsifiable propositions, set them against published evidence that bears on five of them, give a pre-registration-ready design for the proposition on which the epistemic tier rests, and compare the architecture with adjacent frameworks. The paper reports no new experiments. Its contribution is the theory, the formal grounding of its normative tier, an account of what existing evidence already shows, and a program for testing the rest.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) makes it harder to infer a student’s own capability from a submitted product, so assessment increasingly needs evidence of how students reason and regulate their learning. This study examined four questions. Which assessment practices do higher education educators publicly report, and how do they describe their implementation? Which cognitive-engagement and self-regulated learning (SRL) processes are these practices intended to elicit? How does a framework derived from these reports fare against separately sampled external documents? Methods Public posts and comments were collected with TinyFish from Reddit (the principal source), Hacker News, Stack Exchange, Lemmy and Mastodon, covering December 2022 to October 2026. Of 29,355 unique records, 13,903 were eligible, and 5,091 reported or discussed at least one of 11 assessment practices (75.2% from Reddit; 3,741 in educator voice; 1,336 threads). Records were coded with transparent dictionaries, which were validated against an independent model-based coder on a hold-out sample (any practice: κ = 0.49; implemented vs. proposed: κ = 0.69). A seven-component framework built from the corpus was then appraised against 40 external documents not used in its construction. Results Detection and sanction (43.2%) and supervised in-class tasks (28.5%) dominated discussion. Detection’s share fell from 56.4% in 2023 to 37.6% in 2026, while oral, process-based and stakes-related practices roughly doubled. Reasoning was the intended process described most often, yet only 2.2% of records mentioned planning, monitoring and reflection or revision together. Several practice–mechanism associations were largely lexical: reflection vocabulary accompanying reflective tasks fell from 94.2% to 5.5% when shared words were masked. Learning-oriented records described monitoring, application and reasoning more often than detection-only records. The framework described all 40 external documents (13 implemented cases, 13 institutional guidance documents, 14 commentaries; mean fit 3.9/5). However, those documents emphasised authentic task design and reflection rather than secured checkpoints, and they prompted an eighth component, student co-design and transparency. Discussion Public discussion favours securing assessment over making learning visible, and no single practice is described as eliciting both cognitive engagement and a connected SRL cycle. This supports combining complementary forms of evidence. The study documents patterns in public reporting and offers a provisional design framework; it does not measure students’ cognition or learning outcomes.

Background: Spherical trigonometry is essential for maritime navigation; however, conventional instruction often emphasizes procedural drills without connecting mathematical formulas to authentic bridge operations. Objective: This study examined changes in nautical cadets’ learning outcomes and perceived learning experiences following a contextualized Problem-Based Learning (PBL) intervention in spherical trigonometry. Methods: A quantitative quasi-experimental study using a One-Group Pretest–Posttest Design was conducted with 65 nautical cadets at Politeknik Pelayaran Sorong during the 2025/2026 academic year. The PBL intervention integrated authentic Great Circle navigation problems, manual calculations using the Spherical Law of Cosines, and digital cross-checking. Data were collected using pretest and posttest instruments, navigation task evaluations, and a 50-item perception questionnaire. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Modified Normalized Gain (N-Gain), and effect size (image). Results: Learning outcomes increased significantly, with the mean score rising from 59.45 (SD = 19.95) to 71.32 (SD = 22.18) (image), indicating moderate improvement (Modified N-Gain = 0.340) and a moderate-to-large effect size (image). Cadets demonstrated high computational consistency between manual and digital methods, with differences ranging from 0.000% to 0.050%. They also reported positive perceptions of conceptual understanding, motivation, self-directed learning, and collaboration, despite a slight descriptive decline in perceived problem-solving confidence. Conclusion: Contextualized PBL was associated with improved learning outcomes and high computational consistency. Given the single-group design, these findings indicate changes associated with the intervention rather than establishing definitive causality. Controlled, multi-institutional studies are recommended.

As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) plays an increasing role in K-12 mathematics classrooms, understanding how teachers collaborate with these technologies during instructional design is essential. Drawing on frameworks related to personalization theory, Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge, and adaptive epistemic agency, this study examined how seven seventh-grade mathematics teachers interacted with ChatGPT to personalize mathematics word problems to students’ interests. Analyses of teacher-GenAI interactions identified three interaction styles: AI-Dominated-Passive Prompt Personalization, Teacher-Dominated-Rigid Personalization, and Human-AI partnership-Collaborative Personalization. Students' ratings of the resulting personalized problems varied across teachers and interaction styles, with the strongest positive patterns occurring among teachers characterized by Collaborative Personalization. Collaborative personalization illustrates how teachers may maintain epistemic authority for evaluating mathematical, pedagogical, and contextual appropriateness while selectively granting GenAI generative authority to expand personalization possibilities. These findings highlight the importance of preparing teachers to critically evaluate and collaboratively engage with GenAI during instructional design.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

The typical workflow for improving large-scale ranking and recommendation models is slow and tedious: an engineer forms a hypothesis, implements it as a code change, trains a model, and evaluates it both offline and online, often relying on their own intuition and experience along the way. Autonomous LLM agents promise to speed this up by running the loop on their own, but it is still unclear whether they can do this in industry-scale systems rather than on benchmarks or small proxy tasks. We build human-on-the-loop machine learning engineer (MLE) agents that propose, implement, train, and evaluate model changes on large-scale search rankers. Engineers retain control over objective design, search direction, and final-model review. We identify three obstacles that make this industry setting challenging: feedback takes hours per experiment, offline metrics do not always predict online impact, and improvements saturate after the early wins. We address these with parallel training runs, an objective calibrated to match online impact, and careful context engineering. In one campaign, the system ran 1,097 completed candidate experiments and accepted 325, a 29.6\% acceptance rate compared with 15.6\% in the earlier campaign under a different objective and search constraint. Its best model increases search volume by 0.23\% in an A/B test of large scale. Several improvements were architectural changes the team had never tried, drawn from the broader industry and literature, suggesting that MLE agents can explore regions of the design space that human intuition overlooks. We find that the design of the harness around the model matters: intuition suggests that a stronger underlying model is enough, but in our experience, the design of the loop around it is just as critical. More broadly, our work shows that autonomous agents can do real machine-learning engineering in industry-scale systems.

Psychosocial hazards are established antecedents of psychological strain among construction personnel, yet whether that strain transmits exposure to safety compliance or exposure acts on compliance directly has rarely been tested with criteria sensitive to construct redundancy. This study tested these competing accounts in Pakistan, where construction carries about twice its workforce share of occupational injuries. A questionnaire survey obtained 196 responses, of which 157 were retained after screening for unengaged and duplicate cases. Partial least squares structural equation modeling was applied, with discriminant validity assessed by the heterotrait–monotrait ratio, mediation evaluated through specific indirect effects, and predictive relevance assessed out of sample. Four construct pairs exceeded the discriminant criterion before remediation, one at unity. Psychosocial stressor exposure predicted perceived strain-related safety impairment (β = 0.676) and compliance maintained under strain (β = −0.301), whereas impairment did not predict compliance and the indirect effect spanned zero under both reflective and formative specifications of exposure. Role and employment insecurity predicted compliance positively (β = 0.600), contrary to expectation. Contractors and site managers can monitor workload, scheduling, and communication conditions as early indicators of non-compliance without clinical assessment, regulators should treat work organization and employment security as safety determinants, and compliance observed under job insecurity should not be read as internalized safety commitment.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: La incorporación de inteligencia artificial generativa en la educación media plantea una tensión entre su potencial de apoyo y el riesgo de sustituir procesos cognitivos esenciales. El objetivo de este estudio fue diseñar un modelo pedagógico mediado por inteligencia artificial generativa que promueva pensamiento crítico y aprendizaje significativo en estudiantes de educación media colombiana, bajo una perspectiva humanocéntrica de Sociedad 5.0. Se desarrolló una investigación cualitativa, documental, interpretativa y teórico-propositiva. El corpus estuvo compuesto por 40 fuentes: 35 sustantivas y cinco metodológicas, examinadas mediante ocho categorías y una ruta de diez fases. La síntesis produjo ocho hallazgos documentales y sustentó CRISOL-IA 5.0, integrado por diez principios, siete componentes y seis fases: Contextualizar, Recuperar, Interrogar, Someter a contraste, Organizar y Lograr transferencia. Su funcionamiento se representó en una secuencia demostrativa de cuatro sesiones para grado décimo, con seis evidencias observables. La comprobación conceptual mostró cobertura de las seis fases y los siete componentes; de nueve criterios funcionales, seis se cumplieron en el diseño, dos quedaron condicionados por el contexto institucional y uno —eficacia educativa— requiere aplicación con participantes. Se concluye que el aporte ofrece una arquitectura pedagógica trazable y adaptable, sin constituir todavía una validación empírica.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The U.S. reproductive health landscape is fragmented, with legal, digital, and interpersonal privacy risks that are highly contextual and often poorly addressed by conventional privacy guidance. Prior work has proposed narrative threat modeling as an alternative to predominantly technical approaches to reproductive privacy communication. Building on this work, we introduce narrative threat zine-ing , a qualitative method that invites participants to communicate reproductive privacy through story and form rather than checklists or technical instruction. We report findings from four zine-making workshops in which participants created zines for people they worried about in the post- Roe landscape. Participants consistently framed reproductive privacy through relationships, lived experience, and storytelling, positioning zines as tools for awareness, solidarity, and collective sensemaking rather than prescriptive guidance. We argue that narrative threat zine-ing offers a method for examining how people interpret and communicate reproductive privacy under conditions of legal and social uncertainty.

Developing autonomous agents to deal with real-world problems is challenging, especially when developers are not necessarily specialists in artificial intelligence. Recent advances in machine learning for natural language processing tasks are reaching performance levels suitable for practical applications, although these approaches rely on opaque, inscrutable models. This poses three key challenges: the interface between the programming and the developer, the efficiency of the resulting agents, and the scrutiny of their behaviour. We tackle the challenge of developing autonomous agents over natural language environments in an efficient agent architecture that leverages recent developments in natural language processing and the intuitive folk psychology abstraction of the beliefs, desires, intentions (BDI) architecture. This paper introduces NatBDI , a new class of agent architecture that uses the BDI reasoning cycle with components driven by natural language processing. This allows a developer to instruct the agent more directly using a combination of controlled natural language structure and natural language knowledge as its programming interface. The resulting architecture handles natural language environments using a combination of language models and natural language inference to bootstrap the agent’s reasoning. We empirically assess the efficiency gains of this combination while introducing a more intuitively programmed autonomous agent. Instructions in this interface substantially improve agent performance in the experimental scenario over a baseline agent created using a pure machine learning approach. The resulting architecture shows that combining learned policies with intuitively engineered domain knowledge yields substantial performance gains. We expect this class of agents to provide a powerful, yet intuitive, tool for agent-driven programming.

documents.abstract: AI-generated review summaries are reshaping how consumers access product information, but their influence also extends to consumers who write reviews. Examining Amazon’s rollout of AI-generated review summaries, we find that these summaries encourage more review contributions and richer content. Consumers discuss product attributes absent from the summaries and elaborate on topics already covered. A controlled experiment suggests that summaries strengthen consumers’ belief that their contributions, together with others’, help future buyers make informed decisions. The increase in review contributions is stronger for products with many existing reviews or mixed ratings. Platform managers could prioritize summaries for products with mixed ratings, for which additional reviews can provide a more complete picture for future buyers. To build on richer review content, platforms could use writing prompts that highlight product attributes underrepresented in AI summaries. However, additional analyses suggest that AI summaries disproportionately benefit products that already sell well, potentially reinforcing sales concentration. Platforms could increase exposure for niche or new products, whereas policymakers could encourage fairness standards and periodic assessments of how AI-generated summaries affect product visibility and sales concentration. These findings highlight the potential of AI summaries to encourage consumer contributions, drawing attention to the risk of increased sales concentration.

This study examined how profiles of perceived teacher emotional support, helplessness, and self-efficacy for managing personal difficulties were associated with agentic engagement among Kuwaiti adult university students during wartime. Survey responses were collected from 546 students in higher education through a cross-sectional design. The stress measure referred to the wartime period and did not directly assess war exposure or trauma. Confirmatory factor analysis supported the measurement model. Latent profile analysis identified three profiles. These were Supported-Strained, Low-Support/Lower-Efficacy, and Low-Helplessness/High-Efficacy. Comparisons that accounted for classification uncertainty showed significantly lower agentic engagement in the Low-Support/Lower-Efficacy profile than in both other profiles. The Supported-Strained and Low-Helplessness/High-Efficacy profiles did not differ significantly in the primary analysis. After adjustment for gender, however, agentic engagement was significantly higher in the Supported-Strained profile. The findings suggest that agentic engagement during wartime differs across combinations of perceived support and psychological experiences. Greater helplessness did not consistently coincide with lower engagement. These cross-sectional associations do not establish that teacher support or wartime conditions caused the differences.

Characteristics of Artificial Intelligence (AI) severely restrict human control. This creates new challenges for socio-technical systems design especially in safety-critical domains, where control over risks is essential along with the accountability for any harm caused. Drawing from human factors and AI governance literature, expert interviews and participant observation in a complex high-risk AI use case from the railways, we developed ALIGN, a scenario-based method that supports the governance of and stakeholder involvement in AI development and implementation in three ways: raising awareness for potential accountability-control misalignments in socio-technical systems and their negative consequences, offering a structured approach to assessing the alignment between accountability and control for stakeholders in a given use case, and supporting effective design decisions to mitigate AI risks. We describe the iterative development and evaluation of ALIGN and discuss how this method promotes AI governance by highlighting the relevance of control-accountability alignment throughout the AI life cycle.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Who is accountable for what an AI system does, and how can that accountability be shown rather than asserted? Human sign-off and the autonomous agent both place the last word in a single party. Following a design science approach, we built and used a third arrangement, the verification interface: human, machine and an explicit ethics core form one construct, the core has the last word over both, and every output carries a tamper-evident receipt showing what was checked. The interface has been in daily use since February 2026 and had issued 12,398 receipts by 10 October 2026. In a sealed blind test on 1798 AI answers checked against company records, its verdicts matched the answer key in 97.1% of cases; a human check of 50 answers on which two AI auditors disagreed confirmed the answer key in 44. A check took a median of 1.9 s. We derive seven design requirements, report which the interface meets, and connect the approach to EU2122, a public content profile for receipts published as an IETF Internet-Draft. The economic hypothesis, that verification per output removes the review bottleneck of AI adoption and raises speed, quality and operating margin together, is stated but not tested. The interface assumes neither that AI is conscious nor that it has moral standing. All evidence comes from one system and is reported by its developer; it shows feasibility and measured accuracy in one domain, not effectiveness across organisations.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Low back pain (LBP) is a common occupational health problem among healthcare workers. While physical demands are known to contribute to LBP, few large-scale studies have investigated the contribution of psychosocial stressors. This study examined the association between occupational LBP and stress-related factors at a university hospital in Japan. In this cross-sectional study, we analyzed responses to the Brief Job Stress Questionnaire administered to 2,450 staff members. Participants were categorized into LBP and non-LBP groups. The prevalence of LBP and high stress was compared by occupation. Multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors independently associated with LBP. The overall prevalence of frequent LBP was 29.1%, being highest in nurses (39.3%) and lowest in doctors (11.1%). The odds ratio for LBP in nurses versus doctors was 3.54 (95% confidence interval 2.22–5.63). High stress status was more common in the LBP group than in the non-LBP group (25.1% versus 6.9%). Multivariate analysis showed that subjective physical workload, interpersonal stress in the workplace, physical fatigue, depressive symptoms, support from supervisors, work/life satisfaction, and body mass index were independently associated with LBP. These findings provide epidemiological evidence that both physical and psychosocial stressors are associated with occupational LBP among healthcare workers.

Background Maintaining safe workplace environments in manufacturing industries is important for ensuring employees' health and maintaining effective production performance. Research on environmental safety and occupational health and safety is extensive, but the association between environmental safety and production efficiency and whether employees' safety knowledge supports this relationship, has received limited attention. Methods Data were collected from two independent cross-sectional purposive samples of footwear production workers (Wave 1 and Wave 2; N = 385 each), 3 months apart, and analyzed separately using Hayes PROCESS macro model 7 to investigate the indirect association between environmental safety and production efficiency through occupational health and safety, and the moderating effect of safety knowledge, with a simple slope test used to probe the interaction. Total effects were estimated using model 4. Results Contrary to the hypothesized direction, the association between environmental safety and occupational health and safety was weaker at higher safety knowledge in both waves; the interaction was significant after correction for multiple testing in Wave 1 only. In Wave 1, the interaction was a crossover: environmental safety was positively related to occupational health and safety only at low safety knowledge, and the indirect effect on production efficiency was significant only at low safety knowledge. The direct and total effects were not significant. In Wave 2, environmental safety was positively related to occupational health and safety at all levels of safety knowledge, with the association weakening as knowledge increased. The indirect effect was significant at low, mean and high safety knowledge, and the direct and total effects were also significant, indicating partial mediation. Conclusion In both waves, environmental safety was indirectly associated with production efficiency through occupational health and safety, at least among workers with lower safety knowledge, and this indirect association was weaker among workers with higher safety knowledge. These cross-sectional findings suggest that safe working environments may be particularly relevant for workers with lower safety knowledge.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

Background. Ambient clinical AI — software that listens to a consultation and drafts the clinical note, often called an AI scribe — is now a flagship use of artificial intelligence in healthcare. Most tools delivering it are proprietary and cloud-based: consultation audio leaves the building, errors cannot be independently characterised, and the clinician who signs the note answers for output nobody outside the vendor can examine. Open, fully local alternatives that a clinician or researcher can inspect, run and modify remain rare. Objective. This paper reports OpenConsult, an open-source AI scribe with live clinical decision support that runs entirely on one machine in the consulting room and is inspectable end to end, and describes its formative evaluation. Methods. Evaluation was formative and used synthetic consultations only (scripted and acted). Automated tests ran fifteen scripted consultations with pre-written marking schemes, checking transcription quality gates, the urgency alarm’s behaviour across emergency and routine scripts, and whether every cited claim in a note points to a real transcript line. Five acted consultations followed in a real consulting room, and the AI assistants that built the system ran an adversarial security audit under the developer’s direction. The work is reported against the applicable DECIDE-AI items, one stage before live clinical evaluation. Results. OpenConsult is a fully local, open-source consultation assistant, built by a practising general practitioner directing AI coding assistants, running on a single consumer graphics card. It transcribes the consultation live and separates the speakers, drafts a structured clinical note with every sentence linked to its supporting transcript words, runs live decision support whose urgency alarm is shown only to the doctor, drafts referral letters, and offers a supervised spoken history-taking mode. In generated notes, 301 of 302 citations pointed to real transcript lines — an existence check, with clinical faithfulness unmeasured pending independent rating; the one uncited claim was flagged for manual checking. The urgency alarm fired in all eight scripted emergencies and stayed silent in six of seven routine consultations. Five acted consultations surfaced five defects the automated checks had missed, four of them serious; all were fixed, each pinned by a regression test. The security audit returned twelve findings, including one critical vulnerability, fixed and verified before any public exposure. Conclusions. OpenConsult is a working, auditable proof of concept — not yet a validated clinical tool — released for research and education only, with real patient care out of scope. It is intended as an open research instrument: it records whether the reviewing clinician opened the cited evidence before approving, how long review takes, and every revision of its decision support, making human review of ambient clinical AI measurable. Independent, prospective evaluation is required before any step toward care.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Technology and Human Factors in Education and Health

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is entering the everyday work of secondary schools. Teachers encounter AI-based tools both in classroom organisation and in feedback or adaptation tasks. As these tools become more visible in school practice, their educational role and practical value need to be examined in relation to the conditions of real classrooms. This is especially relevant in classes with varied learning characteristics, where students differ in pace and readiness to participate. In these settings, AI may help teachers adapt instructional material and provide more individualised support. Its value, however, depends on professional judgement and on how each tool is connected to pedagogical purpose. This paper examines opportunities and challenges related to the use of artificial intelligence in secondary education. The planned study will use teachers’ accounts to examine how AI tools are understood and used in secondary school practice. It is designed as a qualitative inquiry based on semi-structured interviews with secondary education teachers, with the interview material examined thematically. Through teachers’ accounts, the study will explore how AI is understood in relation to lesson preparation and student support, while also examining what makes its use difficult in day-to-day teaching. The paper approaches AI as a tool whose usefulness depends on classroom context and teachers’ pedagogical decisions.

documents.abstract: Virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) are moving from experimental demonstrations to operational tools in military aviation. This article examines the main opportunities these technologies offer in six areas: immersive flight and mission training, cockpit and helmet-mounted displays, live-virtual-constructive training, aircraft maintenance, mission planning and debriefing, and human-performance training. Using an analytical review of academic and professional literature, the study compares the potential benefits of each application area with its principal technical and human-factors limitations. The findings show that VR offers the clearest near-term value in cost-effective procedural and tactical training, while AR offers the greatest long-term value in airborne information display and in maintenance support. Simulator sickness, latency, registration accuracy, cybersecurity and the need for validated transfer-of-training evidence remain the key barriers. The article concludes with practical recommendations for armed forces and military education institutions that wish to adopt these technologies in a phased and evidence-based way.

Explainable AI (XAI) is frequently applied to high-stakes tabular data, yet the field relies heavily on feature attribution methods. While these approaches offer technical transparency, evaluating dozens of isolated features demands excessive cognitive effort from non-expert users. In this paper, we argue that prototypes remain overlooked and underutilized, and should be integrated as a complementary, intuitive gateway to auditing complex machine learning models. Although entire exemplars function as an intuitive baseline for prototype-based explanations, we highlight prototypical parts as particularly valuable for tabular data. By grouping related features into bounded subspaces, prototypical parts technically embody human-understandable concepts, replacing isolated features with cohesive semantic units. We support this integration through two primary lenses. Cognitively, these parts align with Rosch's categorization theory and Kahneman's System 1 thinking to naturally reduce cognitive load for humans. Then, we introduce a Geometric Validity Triad to conceptualize why prototypes validate the data manifold - a critical dimension often neglected by existing methods. We contend that making tabular XAI genuinely comprehensible requires shifting toward composite explanation pipelines that pair intuitive similarity-based reasoning with rigorous feature-level auditing. The paper concludes by outlining open challenges of prototype-based methods and discussing potential solutions to guide future research.

Academic stress among university students is commonly linked to heavy assignment loads, yet the role of time management in this relationship remains contested. This study examines the effects of assignment workload and time management on academic stress and tests time management as a moderator. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted among active students of Universitas Pamulang, Indonesia (n = 37, purposive sampling) using a five-point Likert questionnaire, and analysed with multiple regression and moderated regression. Assignment workload had a positive and significant effect on academic stress (β = 0.734, p < .001), whereas time management had no direct effect once workload was controlled (β = 0.081, p = .552). The model explained 62.0% of the variance in academic stress. Time management significantly weakened the workload–stress relationship (interaction b = −0.308, p = .002, ΔR² = .095). The study positions time management as a buffer rather than a direct predictor. Universities should combine coordinated scheduling of assignments with proactive time-management support.

Over the past decade, the innovative convergence of cloud computing, natural language processing (NLP), and large language models (LLM) has triggered a paradigm shift in human-computer interaction. This study aims to conceptually review and propose a research design to objectively analyze the effect of security and privacy perceptions on the use of AI as a venting medium. The proposed method is a conceptual quantitative research design with a correlational approach, planned for Generation Z respondents. Based on a literature synthesis of referenced studies, the findings indicate a highly significant positive correlation between dispositional shame and self-disclosure to artificial intelligence (r = 0.337, p < 0.001, n = 182). The conceptual review concludes that AI operates effectively as a complementary screening instrument but risks triggering an atrophy of social resilience, thus necessitating juridical protection through the Personal Data Protection Law (UU PDP).
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Amaç: Bu çalışma, insan merkezli bakım ile işgücü refahı, hasta güvenliği ve sağlık hizmetlerinde kalite yönetimi arasındaki kavramsal bağlantıları aydınlatmak ve insan merkezli kalite yönetişiminin kavramsal bir modelini geliştirmek amacıyla ISO 7101:2023 standardına yönelik nitel bir belge analizi yapmayı amaçlamıştır. Yöntemler: Çalışmada, Bowen’ın (2009) belge analizi çerçevesine göre nitel kavramsal belge analizi ilkeleri uygulanmıştır. Yöntemler: ISO 7101:2023 standardının 4 ila 10. maddelerinin (kuruluş bağlamı, liderlik, planlama, destek, operasyon, performans değerlendirmesi ve iyileştirme) içerik analizi ve her maddeyle ilgili ifadelerin ilk kodlaması, ardından kodların mantıksal tematik gruplandırılması gerçekleştirilmiştir. Sonuçlar: Altı tema ortaya çıkmıştır: kalite yönetiminin insan merkezli dönüşümü; hizmet kullanıcı deneyimi ve ortak üretim; şefkatli bakım, etik ve kapsayıcılık; işgücü refahı ve sürdürülebilir kalite; hasta güvenliği ve risk kültürü; performans değerlendirmesi ve sürekli iyileştirme. Bulgular: ISO 7101:2023, mevzuata uygunluk ve denetimin ötesine geçen, ilişkisel, etik ve insan merkezli bir düzeyde kavramsal bir çerçeve sunmaktadır. Sonuç: Bulgularımıza dayanarak, sürekli bir döngü içinde uygulanan altı birbirine bağlı boyuttan oluşan “İnsan Odaklı Kalite Yönetişim Modeli”ni öneriyoruz: liderlik ve kalite kültürü, risk temelli düşünme ve etik yönetişim, işgücü refahı ve psikolojik güvenlik, insan odaklı bakım ve ortak üretim, hasta güvenliği ve hizmet kullanıcı deneyimi ile performans değerlendirmesi ve sürekli iyileştirme. Bu çalışma, sağlık hizmetleri kalite yönetimi, hasta güvenliği ve işgücü refahı üzerine mevcut literatüre insan merkezli ve etik bir kalite yönetişim perspektifi sunmakta ve sağlık kuruluşlarının kalite uygulamalarının ISO 7101:2023 standardına uymasına yardımcı olacak bir kavramsal çerçeve sağlamaktadır.Anahtar kelimeler: ISO 7101:2023; sağlık hizmetleri kalite yönetimi; insan merkezli bakım; işgücü refahı; hasta güvenliği; belge analizi; kalite yönetişimi.

Digital inclusion with generative AI depends not only on educators’ access to tools but on how they use them. Comparing the benefits educators perceive with the uses they report may reveal gaps between what educators believe AI can do and how they use it in teaching. In this exploratory secondary analysis of survey data from 293 Minnesota PK-12 and higher education educators, we compared endorsement of improved accessibility for diverse learners as a benefit of generative AI with reported use of AI to enhance accessibility for students with disabilities. Because the items differ in scope and target population, the comparison describes response proportions, not a failure to act on a belief. Among 160 AI-using educators who answered both items, 133 (83.1%) endorsed the benefit and 51 (31.9%) reported the use (McNemar exact p < 0.001). Subgroup differences were not detected, though power was limited. Among all AI users, self-rated competence was associated with reported accessibility use (44.0% vs. 27.9%; adjusted OR = 2.31, 95% CI [1.13, 4.73]); among endorsers, the estimate was imprecise. Keyword-selected open-ended responses more often described general differentiation and language support than disability-specific use. We discuss measurement implications and propose supports as hypotheses for evaluation.

Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in medical training, but evidence from African residency programs is scarce. We assessed how internal medicine residents in Ethiopia use GenAI and how they perceive its impact on clinical learning and clinical decision-making. Methods We conducted an explanatory sequential mixed-methods study consisting of a national cross-sectional online survey of internal medicine residents (June to August 2026), followed by two focus group discussions (FGDs) with 10 residents at two universities (September 2026) to explain the survey findings. Perceived impact was measured with five-point Likert items and two composite scores (learning, five items; decision-making, eight items). Associations with frequency of use were tested with chi-square or Fisher's exact tests. FGD data were organized deductively into categories based on the survey topics. Results Of 252 respondents from 18 institutions, 98.8% had used GenAI and 75.4% used it daily; ChatGPT was used by 91.6% of users. The mean composite score for perceived impact on clinical learning was 3.83 out of 5 (70.7% high) and for clinical decision-making 3.86 out of 5 (67.7% high). Agreement was highest for improved differential diagnosis (90.8%), learning efficiency (81.9%) and support for self-directed learning (79.5%), and lowest for ward-round performance (64.3%) and confidence in complex cases (71.4%). Daily use was more frequent among residents with more than three hours of daily internet use (82.3% versus 66.7% to 67.4%; p = 0.024) and was not associated with age, sex, marital status, year of residency, device access or formal training. In the FGDs, residents described GenAI as a fast, supportive tool for learning and clinical work, as an aid to reasoning and not a replacement for physician judgment, and as a possible threat to independent learning. Conclusions Residents perceive GenAI as helpful for self-directed learning and diagnostic reasoning while keeping final responsibility for clinical decisions. These findings reflect perceptions and not measured outcomes, so objective evaluation of its effects on learning and clinical performance is needed.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has altered how assessment supports learning and evidences achievement in higher education. Early institutional responses concentrated on academic integrity, detection, and task redesign, while a rapidly expanding empirical literature documents the contingent benefits and trade-offs of AI-mediated learning. This conceptual paper develops an assessment-specific framework organised around two dimensions: the distribution of learning-relevant cognitive responsibility and the visibility of student process. GenAI can operate as an engagement amplifier when it supports cognitive and metacognitive activity while preserving student responsibility for the intellectual work that matters, or as a cognitive substitute when it displaces that work while enabling successful task completion. The framework distinguishes immediate AI-supported performance from durable capability, whether demonstrated independently or with GenAI, and connects this distinction to the validity of inferences drawn from assessment evidence. Rather than proposing a universal solution to what has been called the wicked problem of AI and assessment, the framework offers an evaluative lens for judging how particular assessment configurations distribute cognitive responsibility and make student thinking visible, and whether the resulting evidence can support defensible claims about achievement. This reframing informs assessment judgements without prescribing a single model for all higher education contexts.

As artificial intelligence becomes embedded in news production, journalistic credibility can no longer be understood only through audience trust in machine-generated content. This article examines how AI-generated and AI-assisted journalism is made to appear trustworthy through textual, editorial, and institutional cues. Drawing on qualitative comparative content analysis of a 37-text corpus comprising 14 AI-generated or AI-assisted news articles, 14 human-written comparison articles, four newsroom AI policy documents, and five correction or controversy-related texts, the study analyses how credibility is constructed through authorship, disclosure, sourcing, human oversight, correction practice, and institutional framing. The findings show that AI-assisted journalism can reproduce familiar signs of professional news, including factual tone, structured formats, institutional attribution, and data specificity. Yet these cues do not necessarily make editorial responsibility visible. The article develops the concept of algorithmic credibility performance to explain how AI journalism assembles trustworthiness through uneven arrangements of transparency, evidence, and accountability before audiences respond.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the way learners look for information, develop ideas, and complete assignments, which makes it necessary to rethink what independent thinking means. Drawing on the philosophy of education, including Islamic educational philosophy, this article addresses three questions: the nature of learners’ independent thinking, the duality of AI as either a reinforcer of reasoning or a source of intellectual dependency, and the reconfiguration of educators’ roles and learning objectives. The study is a qualitative, descriptive-critical literature review of eleven Indonesian-language journal articles published between 2023 and 2026, supported by foundational theoretical and philosophical works. It argues that AI’s effect on reasoning is not an inherent property of the technology; rather, it is likely to be shaped by the cognitive operations handed over to the machine and by the order in which AI is introduced into a learning task. Dependency is most likely when AI takes over analysis and judgment, and least likely when it is used to explain or to test the learner’s own thinking. Educators are therefore urged to design thinking processes, move assessment from products to processes, and nurture scholarly ethics such as honesty and tabayyun (careful verification). These conclusions are conceptual and call for empirical testing across educational levels.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can expand the range of candidate solutions available during design exploration, but it can also obscure whether students have engaged in the iterative design reasoning and evaluative judgement that studio teaching is intended to develop. This article examines how GenAI can be integrated into creative media education without displacing the cognitive processes through which creative expertise is cultivated. It draws on design research, automation literature, and cognitive load theory, alongside illustrative teaching cases spanning undergraduate and postgraduate animation, visual effects, and game design curricula at Auckland University of Technology and The Hong Kong Polytechnic University. We argue that the educational value of GenAI depends not on the sophistication of its outputs alone, but on whether students retain responsibility for evaluative judgement throughout the design process. We propose Process Before Prompting, a pedagogical framework intended to preserve this responsibility within human-led cycles of divergence, convergence, and appreciative judgement. Students establish an initial creative intention before engaging with GenAI and remain responsible for interpreting, refining, and selecting among both human- and AI-generated candidates. This framework offers practical guidance for scaffolding independent judgement and assessing evidence of iterative design reasoning within existing studio teaching practices.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly becoming embedded in higher education systems, influencing teaching, assessment, research, and institutional decision-making. Despite the growing adoption of AI, existing governance approaches remain largely principle-based, emphasizing ethical guidelines such as transparency, accountability, and fairness without providing operational mechanisms for implementation within quality assurance (QA) and accreditation systems. This creates a critical gap between AI governance principles and the procedural structures through which educational quality and institutional accountability are evaluated. This study addresses this gap by developing an operational quality assurance framework to systematically integrate AI governance into a ten-step higher education accreditation lifecycle, with explicitly differentiated AI permission levels and defined boundaries for human evaluative authority. Using a conceptual and policy-synthesis approach, the study integrates global AI governance principles, established QA standards, and accreditation practices into a risk-based, human-centered governance model. The framework operationalizes AI governance and integration through a model that defines the role, boundaries, and permissible levels of AI use across each stage of the accreditation process. A central feature of the model is the explicit preservation of human decision-making authority in evaluative and high-stakes accreditation stages. The study reconceptualizes AI integration in higher education as a quality assurance and governance challenge rather than solely a technological innovation problem. By embedding AI governance and integrating it directly within accreditation processes, the proposed model provides a practical bridge between ethical principles and operational implementation. The proposed framework provides a structured basis for quality assurance agencies, regulators, and higher education institutions to consider risk-based AI governance within accreditation processes, with its feasibility, effectiveness, and transferability requiring further evaluation through implementation and empirical validation.

There is an ontological shift currently taking place in the modern workplace due to AI and collaborative technologies. The classical theories of human relations, which rely on human interaction and human co-presence, fail to explain the relational issues involved in the modern hybrid human-AI workplace environment. This paper proposes a theoretical framework known as the Post-Human Relations Theoretical Framework (PHRTF). The PHRTF is conceptualised using post-humanist organisational theory, actor-network theory, sociotechnical systems analysis, and sociology of work and technology. In light of the systematic theoretical synthesis and review of empirical papers written between 2015 and 2024, the study finds four interrelated foundations of the post-human relational ecosystem: distributed agency and relational ontology; affective infrastructure and hybrid trust; temporal-spatial dislocation and presence reconstitution; and algorithmic authority and moral accountability. The framework challenges classical human relations’ anthropocentrism, arguing that ethical, productive AI-workplace relationships require a new understanding of relational actors.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a technology with tremendous potential to revolutionize healthcare, contributing to progress in medical diagnostics, clinical decision support, personalized medicine, patient monitoring, medical research, and healthcare management. This systematic review covers the current use of AI in healthcare, its clinical effects and hindrances for implementation. The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines were followed to conduct a systematic literature search. The search query was conducted in major electronic databases using specific keywords of the studies and results, such as PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, and other sources, including studies on artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, generative AI, large language models, healthcare applications, clinical decision support, medical imaging, drug discovery, digital health, and healthcare data systems. This evidence review identifies evidence of how AI is being used in a variety of healthcare areas such as medical imaging and diagnostics, virtual patient monitoring, drug design, precision medicine, rehabilitation, patient engagement, and operational health care processes. The use of AI has been shown to have the potential to enhance the accuracy of diagnosis, improve clinical decision‐making, personalize care, and optimize healthcare workflows. However, there are substantial hurdles to overcome, such as data privacy and security issues, algorithmic bias, the lack of the clinical validation of AI models, regulatory scrutiny, infrastructure challenges, and the need for effective clinical validation. The key takeaways from this review are the need for a balanced approach to the integration of AI in healthcare, acknowledging both the technological innovations and the ethical, regulatory, and human factors considerations that need to be addressed. More large‐scale clinical validation studies are needed as well as the establishment of reliable AI systems and strategies to ensure responsible and fair use of AI in healthcare.

documents.abstract: Working from home (WFH) research typically presents employees’ preferences and companies’ policies for offsite work in an aggregate manner but neglects differences between employees’ rationales in the light of how digital technology has formed their performative interaction in teams. In this paper we argue that the shortcoming results from underestimating the digital artifact as merely a passive job resource. Thus, we explore WFH preferences as contextualized construct reflecting individual, team, and technological characteristics of digital work also in their interrelatedness. Our theoretical framework adopts a sociomaterial perspective that integrates human-centric and team-centric approaches and guides the identification of distinct WFH configurations. The empirical basis consists of two cross-sectional surveys conducted in 2023 ( n = 296) and 2025 ( n = 290) among German-speaking respondents with WFH options. Using exploratory and confirmatory latent profile analyses to substantiate our configurational approach, we identify three different and robust profiles: (1) a Life Balance Profile emphasizing individual interests for offsite work while expecting HR policies supporting individual detachment, (2) a Chronos Profile emphasizing onsite synchrony with colleagues while expecting mandated same office days for all, and (3) a Kairos Profile emphasizing (hybrid) performative interaction and availability in critical moments independently from the work location. Differences between configurations can be explained by employees’ centrality of work, their digital collaboration preferences, their perceived operational team readiness, and digital competences. Notably, similar aggregate preferences for more offsite work go along with different HR policy expectations.

AI evaluation can involve an active, adaptive optimisation process in which AI agents re-plan, retry, use tools or delegate work to achieve a goal. Unanticipated capabilities or unsafe behaviour may emerge, and existing controls may be inadequate to prevent harm. Selected safeguards may also be deliberately relaxed to observe behaviour they would otherwise suppress, creating additional risks. This article examines the distinctive safety considerations of evaluation and their implications for control placement, observation and intervention, and presents four architectural patterns to support safe AI evaluation, including diverse supervisors, an independent verifier, silent monitoring and coordinated shutdown.

documents.abstract: Problem: Safety-in-design decisions are often made before users, operating environments and manual-handling demands are understood. This risks products valued by customers creating avoidable physical demands for staff who handle them. Air New Zealand is collaborating with Auckland University of Technology (AUT) to embed human factors and ergonomics (HFE) in product development. Method: The collaboration engages students from second year to Masters level in manual-handling risk assessment, the hierarchy of controls and ergonomic principles. Students examine products and processes as systems through site-based problem framing, worker input, task analysis and concept review. Two case studies: adaptation of an airline jug, and redesign of the Business Premier mattress. The mattress project, led with a Bachelor of Industrial Design student, mapped its lifecycle: laundry, supply and amenities placement, transport to the aircraft, cabin-crew interaction, storage, offboarding and return to laundry. Whilst second year students did the same with the coffee jug.

documents.abstract: Schools across Asia are experiencing rapid educational change due to technology integration. Teachers increasingly face pressure to use Artificial Intelligence (AI), while also worrying about errors, cheating, ethical concerns, and unclear institutional policies. This study explored school leaders’ perceptions of how teachers experience AI-related anxiety and how leadership practices support teachers’ AI competence in South Asian countries. A phenomenological research design was employed. Using purposive and snowball sampling, 10 high school leaders from Pakistan, Sri Lanka, India, Bangladesh, and Nepal were selected. Data were collected online through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using thematic analysis. Four themes emerged from the findings. First, school leaders perceived that teachers feared accountability and public criticism when AI-generated outputs were inaccurate or inappropriate. Second, school leaders reported that teachers expressed concerns about cheating, fairness, and loss of professional identity. Third, school leaders described reducing teachers’ anxiety by creating low-risk professional learning environments and encouraging peer support. Fourth, leaders established clear guidance regarding acceptable AI use, transparency, and student data protection. Across the participating schools, leaders consistently viewed teachers’ AI-related anxiety as a major barrier to responsible AI adoption. The findings suggest that leadership practices supporting ethical AI governance, collaborative professional learning, and equitable AI implementation contribute to sustainable teacher professional development and responsible educational transformation.

People around the globe have moral values and principles. These moral values and principles govern society, since no human society practices a free-rider system. These rules and regulations form the foundation of the public good and general well-being of every society, as far as social order is concerned. Social Order, the matrix of human relationships in society, arises from the context of human nature. Human nature includes many social attributes and characteristics, such as ways of thinking and empathy. Replacing human contact with the technological term Artificial Intelligence (AI) raises serious social and ethical concerns. Ethics developed and is used because humans are corporeal, vulnerable, and empathetic. These characteristics are the basis of human social nature and, hence, societal ethics. Therefore, this paper examines the social and ethical dimensions of artificial intelligence (AI) in modern society. The new normal, termed artificial intelligence (AI), poses significant social and ethical challenges that demand careful consideration. It can transform our society positively or negatively. To achieve this study's objective, the paper uses a phenomenological and sociological approach, theoretically framed by human nature theory. The study observes that while artificial intelligence (AI) can bring significant benefits to society, it will also affect social attributes such as thinking and empathy that human nature is endowed with. Brotherhood will be completely erased, and family ties and closeness will be destroyed. The work, however, suggests that AI must be built to align with humanity's overarching goals.

documents.abstract: Digital platforms increasingly mediate urban food provisioning, but their governance architectures may create uneven conditions of participation, visibility and value creation. This study examines how Critical and Emerging Information Technologies (CEIT), digital dynamic capabilities and platform participation are associated with care-oriented value creation among neighbourhood food businesses in Medellín, Colombia. Using an exploratory-descriptive, theory-building design, the study combines a contextual documentary review with descriptive survey data from 100 businesses. The findings show partial and functionally concentrated digitalisation: transactional practices such as digital payments are relatively widespread, whereas integration with e-commerce platforms, logistics systems and advanced digital-management tools remains limited. At the same time, socially embedded value-creation practices, particularly food donations, persist but are weakly formalised and digitalised. These patterns provide evidence of limited platform participation rather than direct evidence of platform exclusion. Building on them, the study develops a relational sociotechnical model in which platform exclusion is theoretically proposed as an endogenous intervening mechanism linking CEIT configurations and digital dynamic capabilities with value-creation outcomes, while recursive mechanisms connect digital traceability, technological visibility and capability renewal. The study contributes by distinguishing digital adoption from platform inclusion, empirical participation from theoretically inferred exclusion, and socially embedded value creation from its digital visibility.
Article published in Junior Journal, volume 9.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used by students for academic support, but it remains unclear how students value AI-based support compared with other forms of teaching and peer support. This study examined learning-support preferences among 366 second-year computing students at Kaunas University of Technology who were surveyed in 2025 and 2026 using a repeated cross-sectional design. Ten learning-support preferences and GenAI use frequency were analyzed using non-parametric tests, equivalence tests, rank correlations, and ordinal logistic regression. Students rated practical examples, clearly structured information, and peer assistance highest, whereas preference for using AI tools in learning was moderate and social media was rated lowest. Between the 2025 and 2026 Software Systems cohorts, weekly or daily GenAI use increased from 58.1% to 77.1%, yet all ten preferences were statistically equivalent across cohorts and across computing programs. More frequent GenAI use was associated with stronger preference for AI-supported learning (ρ = .284; OR = 1.93, 95% CI [1.58, 2.35]), whereas its associations with peer support, group work, and most other forms of support were negligible. The findings suggest that GenAI currently functions as an additional source of learning support rather than a replacement for teaching and peer support.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence is defined in various ways. A machine that enables a more effective way to replace humans in the labor market is one way to define AI. Evaluating external inputs and using it to tackle specific tasks is another way to see AI. With the diversity of definitions, artificial intelligence is generally understood as a tool that helps solve problems, be it personal or professional. Several years ago, before the release of AI applications, people observed how AI worked via personal assistants: Cortana, Siri etc. This is how AI was used at its early stages. Companies started to adopt AI to excel manufacturing and operational tasks, minimizing expenses for labor and excluding human factor at production. Some implement AI for demand and forecast purposes. Sectors of government use AI for their own needs. Healthcare sector with the help of AI improve accuracy of determining patients' diagnoses, massive data facilitates more appropriate personal treatment. In the education sector AI is limited, because it exposes students to losing critical thinking and autonomy. However, students are being taught how to use AI, their knowledge about the technology is being greatly expanded. Focusing on fundamental principles of AI facilitates student's involvement in AI-use. In manufacturing the technology has established its efficacy, through forecast tools, machine-deviation analysis in workflow. Given its moderate cost AI became primary tool not only within big companies, but also amongst small and medium-sized manufacturers.

Many older adults come from culturally and linguistically diverse (CALD) communities, where they frequently interact with people and services in multiple languages. Language translation technology can support their multilingual communication. This scoping review examines research on technology-mediated verbal language translation for older adults and provides recommendations for future research and practice. We identified 41 studies across six databases discussing the considerations, development, implementation, and evaluation of various technologies, including mobile apps, artificial intelligence, social robots, internet of things, and handheld translators. Research shows that current technologies offer better accessibility and availability than human interpreters and enable useful functions, including multimodal instant translation, flexible formats, and personalized features. Nevertheless, limitations remain, including mistranslations, disrupted communication, usability concerns, and technical issues. Our findings provide important evidence on the current landscape, opportunities, and considerations for future design (e.g., accuracy, usability, flexibility) and implementation (e.g., environmental control, technical appropriateness, adequate learning) of this technology.

Gamification in higher education has been studied mainly as a means of increasing motivation, engagement, and achievement, with far less attention to how game mechanics contribute to the creative competence of pre-service teachers. This article advances the Acmeological Gamification Framework for Creative Competence Development (AGF-CCD), a testable developmental theory of how gamified learning conditions may contribute to creative professional capability in teacher education. The framework was developed through a purposive narrative theory-building synthesis, supported by a mechanism-level evidence map in which empirical studies, syntheses, and theoretical sources are kept apart; it is neither a systematic review nor an empirical validation. It takes the well-supported link from need-supportive mechanics to autonomous motivation as a boundary premise and proposes three sequential links: autonomous motivation is channelled by interpretive feedback into reflective practice and in-task metacognitive regulation (P1); reflective practice under psychological safety and meaningful challenge activates divergent and convergent thinking (P2); and repeated, reflected creative activity in authentic professional tasks consolidates into durable creative competence, evidenced by retention and transfer (P3). Three boundary conditions concern the learner (P4a), the design, separating mechanic composition from framing (P4b), and the context, including teaching discipline (P4c). Relative to self-determination theory, the theory of gamified learning, and the interconnected model of professional growth, the framework's distinctive contribution lies in additional mechanisms (feedback architecture and consolidation), predictions that differ from those accounts (cumulative trajectory; reversal under controlling design), and explicit failure conditions. Acmeology is retained only as a falsifiable claim that development is cumulative. A validation roadmap, including a non-gamified reflective control, states how each proposition can be confirmed, qualified, or refuted.

As artificial intelligence service agents (AISAs) become increasingly widespread, anthropomorphism is often proposed as a way to foster user trust, yet empirical findings remain mixed. Drawing on competing trust-building and trust-undermining mechanisms, we conducted a three-level meta-analysis of 211 effect sizes from 136 independent samples ( N = 46,071) to estimate the anthropomorphism–trust association and examine its boundary conditions. The average association was positive and robust to alternative dependence models ( r = 0.462, 95% CI [0.420, 0.502]), but varied substantially across settings (95% prediction interval [−0.131, 0.811]). It was considerably weaker for objectively specified design cues ( r = 0.222) than for perception-based measures ( r = 0.543), most of which captured adjacent trait attributions such as competence and warmth. Restricting outcomes to global trust, reliance, or willingness to depend yielded a similar estimate ( r = 0.475), although construct overlap on the outcome side cannot be ruled out. Cognitive and emotional anthropomorphism were more strongly associated with trust than physical anthropomorphism in aggregate, but this difference was no longer significant after adjusting for operationalization; among design cues, physical and emotional anthropomorphism did not differ significantly, and no design-based cognitive effect sizes were available. The association was stronger in Eastern than in Western samples and in survey than in experimental studies, whereas no statistically significant moderation was detected for gender composition or the prespecified service-context categories. These findings caution against reading the pooled association as a uniform effect of anthropomorphic design and suggest that anthropomorphic cues should complement, rather than substitute for, demonstrable competence and reliability in AISA design and deployment.

documents.abstract: When LLM tools are pushed beyond their capabilities for software development tasks, developers must be able to step in. However, the comprehension that developers acquire during development might be negatively impacted due to excessive code generation. This could create a cognitive debt that needs to be resolved before tasks can be solved efficiently again. We explore how well developers understand code they generated by prompting in comparison to self-written and unseen code and how they reflect on their comprehension. We conduct a crossover experiment and interviews with 35 participants consisting of students, academic personnel, and software developers. After completing two programming tasks with or without LLM chat usage, respectively, participants are tasked with finding introduced mutations in the produced and additional unseen code. We use insights from interviews and screen recordings to supplement our results. Regarding the experiment, 36% of participants report a better understanding of self-written code compared to their generated code. On average, participants solved the comprehension task 20% faster for self-written code than for generated code and found 11% more mutations. Participants needed significantly less time to solve programming tasks when working with the LLM. However, participants with high reliance on the LLM chat and low task engagement showed significantly decreased comprehension. Our qualitative results show great variability in individual perspectives on comprehension differences and strategies to mitigate issues. Strategies for dealing with comprehension differences range from accepting comprehension differences to adapting their LLM interactions or avoiding the tools altogether. Our results warrant further investigation into cognitive debt in larger systems and developer practices to mitigate issues.

This study examines how the deepening of artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics, defined as the progressive replacement of human workers by machines, affects output, employment, poverty and income distribution. Drawing on the economics of prediction and general-purpose technologies, the task-based theory of automation, growth theory, the literature on factor shares and Keynesian demand constraints, we construct a hypothetical economy, Solvania, with 30 million inhabitants, GDP per capita of US$25,000, 6% unemployment, a 5.3% poverty rate and three sectors: agriculture (30% of output and employment), automobile manufacturing (20%) and services (50%). A macro-sectoral model linked to a 150,000-household microsimulation, implemented in Python, traces a gradual scenario, in which automation reaches 25% of jobs within five years and 50% by year 20, and a rapid scenario, in which it reaches 80% in agriculture and manufacturing and 60% in services within ten years. Both paths raise GDP strongly, to US$1.57 trillion by year 20 (gradual) and US$1.39 trillion by year 10 (rapid), but the gains are distributed very unequally. In the rapid scenario unemployment reaches 47.2%, the labour share falls from 60% to 19.9%, the Gini coefficient rises from 0.369 to 0.621 and poverty more than triples to 17.3%, while median income rises by only 8%. A policy package combining an automation levy that finances a universal dividend, universal income support, accelerated reinstatement and work sharing reduces poverty to 0.7%, lowers the Gini to 0.408 and raises GDP by a further 16%. The results are robust to alternative assumptions and support redistributive and labour market institutions established before the fastest phase of automation.
