documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), a data-driven and algorithm-supported technological system, has rapidly expanded its role in transforming daily life and professional practice over the past decade. In this narrative review, the recent literature was examined to evaluate current and emerging applications of AI in veterinary education and practice. A previously reported PubMed-focused search and a broader literature compilation served different purposes. The historical screening counts cannot be fully reconstructed, and the synthesis was narrative rather than systematic. Veterinary schools in the United States and elsewhere have begun exploring and integrating AI into Doctor of Veterinary Medicine (DVM) curricula to support teaching, learning, and competency development. This review summarizes recent advances in the application of AI in veterinary education. In anatomy, AI-based visualization and interactive tools are being explored, although controlled evidence of improved learning outcomes remains limited. In digital pathology, AI-assisted image analysis can provide students with opportunities to develop skills in recognizing and interpreting pathological findings. In clinical settings, AI models have shown potential in selected imaging and clinical-classification tasks, but their educational effectiveness requires further evaluation. Despite these advances, the broader implementation of AI in veterinary education and practice faces important regulatory and ethical challenges, including concerns regarding data privacy, algorithmic bias, academic integrity, and the reliability of AI-generated information. Addressing these issues will require multidisciplinary collaboration, multicenter data integration, appropriate validation, and strong ethical governance. With these foundations in place, AI may serve as a supportive educational and clinical tool rather than a replacement for veterinary educators and professionals. In the future, appropriately validated AI tools may contribute to veterinary education and clinical training.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: AI governance frameworks increasingly rely on the assurance that a “human in the loop” will provide accountability, judgment, and control when artificial intelligence systems are used in consequential decisions. This paper argues that this assurance is incomplete and potentially misleading unless organizations examine whether the human system surrounding the AI is actually capable of exercising judgment when it matters. The paper defines artificial intelligence as machine inference: computational systems that detect patterns, generate outputs, recommend actions, and simulate features of reasoning without conscience, responsibility, embodiment, or wisdom. It introduces the concept of the Empty Chair: the absence of a clearly designated owner for the formation, sustainment, and exercise of human judgment in AI-enabled decision systems. The paper proposes that meaningful oversight requires at least seven conditions: cognitive capability, behavioral authority, relational safety, decision discipline, cognitive sustainment, survivability, and relational sustainment. Drawing on applied organizational work with governance bodies, enterprise leaders, public-facing institutional systems, and cross-organizational cohorts, the paper identifies a recurring capability-authority split in which those most likely to detect certain categories of risk are not always positioned or authorized to interrupt decision momentum. The analysis further examines how automation bias and ethical fading can weaken human responsibility by making AI outputs appear more complete, objective, and procedurally sufficient than they are. The paper reframes cognitive diversity as governance infrastructure rather than a team-building concept and presents the D.E.E.P.E.R.™ practice as a structured method for recurring reflective diversification across decision cycles. It also offers practical interventions, including cognitive diversity audits, cognitive role charters, decision pause points, Empty Chair protocols, authority alignment, and recurring reflective practice. The paper concludes that AI governance cannot stop at governing machines. It must also govern the human systems responsible for supervising them. The central question is not whether a human is present in the loop, but whether that human is formed, positioned, protected, sustained, and authorized to exercise judgment under pressure.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping how extended reality environments are created, experienced, and applied. Advances in generative AI, multimodal foundation models, spatial understanding, embodied intelligence, and wearable technologies create new opportunities across the spatial computing pipeline, but also raise questions concerning human agency, accessibility, trust, and responsible design. This workshop brings together researchers and practitioners from artificial intelligence, computer graphics, human-computer interaction, and extended reality to examine these developments through three complementary perspectives: AI-generated worlds for XR, human-centred interaction, and human augmentation. Invited experts will introduce these perspectives through brief position statements, followed by moderated panel discussions involving speakers and attendees. Interactive breakout sessions will enable participants to identify connections across the three perspectives, discuss open challenges, and formulate promising directions for future research. By combining expert viewpoints with active community participation, the workshop aims to foster interdisciplinary exchange and initiate a broader community effort towards a shared research agenda for the future of AI and XR.

Managerial decision-making is central to organisational effectiveness because it influences resource allocation, employee supervision, operational planning, conflict resolution, and strategic development. In contemporary workplaces, managers are expected to make numerous decisions while handling competing priorities, digital communications, administrative responsibilities, and rapidly changing business conditions. Although decision-making is commonly regarded as a managerial competency, the cumulative demands associated with repeated decisions may receive insufficient attention. Decision fatigue is generally used to describe a perceived decline in decision-making quality, consistency, or willingness following prolonged or demanding decision activity. Its possible manifestations include postponing difficult choices, relying excessively on familiar alternatives, reducing the consideration of available options, and experiencing increased difficulty maintaining attention. However, decision fatigue is not a universally established explanation for all changes in decision performance, and its mechanisms remain subject to scientific debate. The present study examines the hidden costs of decision fatigue in managerial work, with particular attention to managerial judgement and workplace efficiency. It adopts a descriptive and analytical approach based on secondary literature relating to bounded rationality, cognitive workload, selfregulation, information overload, task switching, and organisational decision-making. The analysis explores how repeated decision demands may interact with workplace conditions such as time pressure, frequent interruptions, unclear responsibilities, excessive reporting, and poorly structured approval procedures. It also considers how decision-related difficulties may influence the consistency of managerial evaluations, the timeliness of organisational responses, employee coordination, and the use of resources. The literature-based analysis indicates that decision quality should not be understood as the product of individual mental capacity alone. It is also influenced by expertise, motivation, information quality, organisational culture, task complexity, and the design of decision processes. The study therefore recommends a balanced approach involving decision classification, appropriate delegation, structured evaluation criteria, protected concentration time, better information management, proportionate use of technology, and periodic review of organisational procedures. These measures are proposed as practical management interventions rather than as interventions whose effectiveness has been experimentally established by this paper. The study concludes that organisations should evaluate both the excellence and efficiency of managerial decisions instead of relying exclusively on decision speed or volume. It also identifies opportunities for future empirical research to establish more precisely how decision demands relate to judgement quality and workplace outcomes.

Employee performance is a central determinant of organizational productivity, service quality, and competitiveness, particularly in the fast-changing Malaysian business environment. This paper examines how transformational leadership and organizational culture are theorized and empirically associated with employee performance, and it develops a research framework and testable hypotheses for a survey-based investigation in a selected Malaysian company. Drawing on transformational leadership theory (Bass, 1985; Bass & Riggio, 2006), Schein's model of organizational culture (Schein & Schein, 2017), and social exchange theory (Cropanzano & Mitchell, 2005), the study positions transformational leadership and organizational culture as independent variables and employee performance as the dependent variable. A systematic review of Malaysian and international empirical studies indicates consistent positive associations between transformational leadership behaviors, particularly idealized influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, and individualized consideration, and employee performance outcomes, as well as between supportive organizational cultures and higher performance. The paper details a quantitative, cross-sectional survey design using validated instruments (the Multifactor Leadership Questionnaire, the Organizational Culture Assessment Instrument, and the Individual Work Performance Questionnaire), a Krejcie and Morgan-based sample-size procedure, and a planned analytical strategy combining descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and multiple regression. Four hypotheses are proposed linking transformational leadership and organizational culture, individually and jointly, to employee performance. The paper concludes with theoretical and managerial implications, arguing that Malaysian organizations seeking to improve workforce productivity should invest jointly in leadership development and culture-building initiatives rather than treating them as separate interventions. Limitations of single-organization, cross-sectional designs and directions for future longitudinal and multi-sector research are discussed.

Generative AI functions as a near zero cost execution engine, weakening the long standing reliance on human effort on which traditional intellectual property (IP) systems depend. The academic response has focused, so far, on studying productivity at the micro level, debating the doctrinal question of IP infringement through AI training at the macro level, or blunt denial of AI authorship. These responses miss the central problem: the human provenance at the heart of IP law is now cheap to falsify and hard to verify. In this paper I argue that AI output appropriation poses a significant threat to IP through an adverse selection dynamic. The threat comes from humans who use AI to appropriate its output and extract the value attached to human effort. Skill compression effects cutting across writing, coding, and consulting have begun to commoditize execution, compressing the quality distribution that once supported premium prices for IP protected output. This process is compounded by the difficulty of verifying declared human authorship or inventorship, which may reward deception and discourage honest effort. I therefore explore value migration from execution skill to concentrated complementary assets. Building on market evidence from platform economies, the paper considers an evolution of IP from a rights based asset model to a verification model, in which the human role shifts from creator to authenticator.

Police forces increasingly use Artificial Intelligence in support of specific tasks, such as data analysis, identifying suspects and monitoring public spaces. These uses potentially expand the state’s coercive capacity. Yet we know little about how far people accept these tools across political contexts and how these views systematically relate to other attitudes. We ask whether support rests on views of the technology, the problem AI use addresses, or trust in the institution using it. We analyze a preregistered survey of 9,000 respondents in the United States, China, Taiwan, the United Kingdom, and five EU countries using Bayesian multilevel models. Support is high for most uses everywhere. It rests on general AI benefits, perceived crime trends, and trust in the police, which matters similarly across countries. In contrast, general AI risks, personal fear of crime, and trust in legal institutions play no substantive role on average. Acceptance thus primarily is connected with optimism about AI, a general but not personal sense of problem relevance, and trust in the police.

This article examines the role of artificial intelligence and digital learning platforms in enhancing ESL learners' motivation and engagement in technology-enhanced tasks. It explores how AI-powered applications, interactive learning platforms, personalized feedback, and digital educational resources contribute to students' language development, independent learning, and active participation. Particular attention is given to the influence of artificial intelligence on behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement. The article also discusses the benefits and challenges of integrating digital technologies into English language education and emphasizes the importance of effective pedagogical guidance in creating motivating and learner-centered learning environments.
